Key facts from the book (11 points)
  • Alluvial soils are widespread in the northern plains and the river valleys. These soils cover about 15 lakh sq. km or about 45.6% of the total area of the country.
  • The alluvial soil is largely found in the Indo-Gangetic plain starting from Punjab in the west to the West Bengal and Assam in the east. These soils are also found in deltas of Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery, where they are called deltaic Alluvium. Alluvial soils are formed mainly by Himalayan sediments and sea retreats.
  • The colour of Alluvial soil varies from light grey to ash grey. They vary in nature from Sandy, Loam to Clay.
  • Generally they are rich in Phosphoric Acid, Potash, Lime, and Organic Matter but poor in Nitrogen and Humus content.
  • Due to the cultivation of leguminous crops nitrogen fixation takes place at a faster rate in these soils. They are suitable for irrigation which helps in growing crops like Wheat, Rice, Sugarcane, Jute, Cotton, Maize, Oilseed, Fruits and Vegetables.
  • Generally loamy soil has 40% sand particles, 18% clay particles and 42% silt particles.
  • Types of Alluvial Soil:

Khadar - Khadar is the new alluvium and is deposited by floods annually enriching the soil by depositing fine silts. It always remains fertile.

Bangar - Bangar represents a system of older alluvium deposited away from the flood plains. Its color is pale reddish brown and in this, nodules are formed at large scale.

Bhabar - Bhabar is the gently sloping coarse alluvial zone below the Shiwalik Hills, where streams disappear into permeable sediments.

Tarai - The marshy lowland region south of the Bhabar is called Tarai (Terai). The soil of this region is generally rich in nitrogen and organic matter but poor in phosphate. The ancient alluvial soil found at higher altitudes in this region is known as Rarh Plain.

Alluvial soil → rich in potash, phosphoric acid, alkalies; low in nitrogen; very fertile; covers about 45.6% (15 lakh sq km). Reh, Thur, Chopan are saline soils.

Don't confuse Reh, Thur, Chopan, Kallar are names of saline soils, not alluvial.

  • The soil pH is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity in the soil- pH below 7 is acidic and above 7 is alkaline. Generally, the pH value of crop soil is 6.0-7.0.
  • Acidic soil is sedimentary in nature. It has mixed laterite, ferrous red and another red soil group.
  • These soils are formed by the humid climate, acidic material and geomorphology. Due to temperature, humid climate and heavy rain, rapid erosion occurs in soil and increases the rate of leaching of bases. Due to high temperature with heavy rainfalll, and leaching, acidic soil is formed.
  • Factors causing acidity in the soil include leaching (due to heavy rainfall), acidic substances, acid-forming fertilizers and soluble salts, etc.

Alkali Soil –

  • Generally, the alkaline soil is found in India in dry and wetland regions. It is fromed due to capillary action ofcations such as Mg⁺², Na⁺, Ca⁺⁺, which are deposited on the surface of the soil. This type of soil is mainly distributed in South Punjab, Southern Haryana and West-Rajasthan.
  • Gypsum (CaSO₄) is used to change the alkalinity of the soil and remove the salinity from it.

Chapter 38

Soils · Soil Erosion and Conservation

11 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (16 points)
  • Soil Erosion - The destruction of the soil cover is described as soil erosion. Soil erosion refers to the wearing away and removal of the topsoil by natural physical forces such as water, wind and air.
  • Topsoil is the top layer of soil and is the most fertile because it contains the most organic, nutrient-rich substances.

Causes of Soil Erosion-

(1) Deforestation

(2) Disturbance in the natural drainage pattern, improper design of waterways.

(3) Grazing, Water, Wind, Air

(4) Poor vegetation and cultivation

  • The most affected regions by soil erosion in India are Badlands of the Chambal and Yamuna rivers, Western Himalaya (Shivalik region), Chota Nagpur plateau, Malwa plateau, Black Soil region of Maharashtra, arid regions of Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat. Ravines of Chambal valley are formed by Gully erosion.
  • Splash Erosion: The erosion due to the impact of falling raindrops on soil-surface leading to the destruction of the crumb structure is known as the raindrop or splash erosion. This is the first stage of erosion.
  • Sheet Erosion: Sometimes water flows as a sheet over large areas down a slope. In such cases, the topsoil is washed away. This is known as sheet erosion. It is the second stage of soil erosion.
  • Rill Erosion :- This is the third stage of sheet erosion. If erosion continues unchecked for a sufficient time then rills or small finger-shaped grooves which are a few centimetres in depth may develop on the landscape. Over a period of time, the fine rills increase in number and also become deeper and wider, resembling the twigs, branches and trunk of a tree. This is called rill erosion.
  • Gully Erosion :- This is the fourth stage of erosion. With further erosion of the soil, the rills may become deeper and enlarge the (region between the Tapti and Sabarmati valleys, and are ultimately turning into gullies. Gully erosion is also responsible for the formation of ravines.
  • Stream Channel Erosion :- Water flowing through a channel corrodes its banks and base until a stable base is formed. This form of erosion is known as stream channel erosion.
  • Soil Conservation :- Prevention of soil erosion is also called conservation of soil. The soil erosion can be prevented by promoting afforestation, Crop Rotation, Terrace Farming, Building Dams, Shelter Belts, Ebankments, etc.
  • Crop rotation refers to the practice of growing different types of crops over the same area in different seasons. It enriches soil fertility and helps in pest control. Plants keep soil bound in locks of roots, and thus, prevent soil erosion.
  • Reduced or zero tillage of the land in farming is a way of growing crops or pasture year after year without disturbing the soil through tillage. It helps in soil moisture conservation.

Critical soil erosion → Shivalik/Western Himalayan foothills, Chambal–Yamuna ravines (most affected: Chambal valley), Chotanagpur Plateau, Maharashtra black soil, arid Haryana–Rajasthan–Gujarat. Must know

Chapter 39

Natural Vegetation

38 facts · 3 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (26 points)
  • Natural Vegetation refers to the flora that grows naturally without human aid and they change their physical stability, shape and size with respect to the environment.
  • The Type of vegetation found in an area depends on the geographical factors such as humidity, temperature, soil, rainfall, altitude, etc. On this basis, there are several types of vegetation found in India.

1. Tropical Evergreen Forest-

  • The tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forest is usually found in warm and humid areas receiving more than 200 cm of rainfall and a mean annual temperature above 22° C. The relative humidity of this region is more than 70%.
  • Due to high humidity and temperature, trees are very tall and intensive (dense). They are also called as “Selvas”.
  • There is a different time for leaf fall for different species of trees, due to which the entire forest is evergreen. The tropical evergreen forest in India is found in Assam, Kerala, West Bengal, The Andaman-Nicobar Islands, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram and Western coastal plain.

The major species found in the tropical evergreen forest include Cinchona, Rubber, Coconut, Bamboo, Mahogany, Ebony, etc.

  • 2. Tropical Deciduous or Monsoon Forests:
  • Tropical deciduous forests are also called monsoon forests. Trees shed their leaves in the dry season to conserve water. The average rainfall in this region is 70-200 cm. On the basis of availability of water, these forests can be categorized as Tropical Moist Deciduous Forest and Tropical Dry Deciduous Forest. In India, Tropical Moist Deciduous Forests are found in the eastern slope of the Western Ghats, the northeastern region of the Indian peninsula and the Bhabar and Tarai (Terai) region.
  • Trees found in these forests include Sal, Teak, Neem, Shisham and Mango. Hardwood trees are extremely helpful for making furniture.

3. Tropical Dry Deciduous Forest:

  • These forests are found in the region where there is annual rainfall ranging between 70 and 100 cm. These forests are found mainly in Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
  • The main trees are Rosewood, Mango, Sandalwood, and Mahua. These forests are economically important and valuable.

4. Arid Forest:

  • Arid forests are also referred to as ‘Tropical Thorn Forests’. They are found in the areas receiving less than 70 cm rainfall.
  • They include semi-arid areas of south-west Punjab, South-west Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat.
  • These forests consist of a variety of grasses and shrubs. In these forests, plants remain leafless for most of the year. Important species found are babool, ber, wild date palm, khair, neem, khejri, palas, etc.

5. Delta Forest :-

  • Deltaic forest is also known as mangrove, swampy or littoral forest. Mangroves grow along the coast in the salt marshes, tidal creeks, mudflats and estuaries. Deltaic forest develops in the deltaic regions of the Ganga, Godavari, Brahmaputra, Krishna rivers, etc. The Sundarban forest is the best example of a deltaic forests.

6. Montane Forests:-

In mountainous areas, the decrease in temperature with increasing altitude leads to a corresponding change in natural vegetation. Mountain forests can be classified into two types: the northern mountain forest and the southern mountain forest.

  • The Himalayan range shows a succession of vegetation from tropical to tundra.

Deciduous types of forests are found in the foothills of the Himalayas. It is succeeded by the wet temperat type of forests between an altitude of about 1000-2000m. Evergreen broad leaftrees such as oak and chest nut are predominantly found here. At about 2000-3000m altitude on the southern slopes of the Himalayas, temperate forests containing coniferous trees like Pine, Deodar, Silver Fir, Spruce and Cedar are found. These forests are also found in places with high altitudes in southern and north-east India.

  • Alpine forests grow all along the Himalayas at altitudes ranging between about 3000-4900 meters. Deodar, a highly valued endemic species grows mainly in the western part of the Himalayan range at an altitude of about 1500-3000 meter.
  • The southern mountain forests include the forests found in three distinct areas of the peninsula e.g. the Western Ghats, the Vindhyas and the Nilgiris. Chapter 40

Irrigation and Canals

34 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (22 points)
  • India is situated in tropical, sub-tropical and temperate climate area. The maximum area of the country comes under a high-temperature zone, except for the western Himalayas, north-eastern-Assam, Meghalaya and some parts of South India.
  • High evaporation occurs due to high temperatures. Therefore, there is a need for irrigation to fulfill the deficit of moisture in sown crops.
  • As per Land Use Statistics for 2022- 23, the net irrigated area during 2022-23 was 79312 thousand hectares, out of which 22.85% was accounted by canal source of irrigation, 2.82% by tanks, 49.34% by Tube wells, 13.46% by other well and remaining 11.53% is irrigated by other source of irrigation. The gross irrigated area in 2022-23 was estimated at 122294 thousand hectares, which was 55.75% of the gross cropped area. Indian irrigation projects can be classified into three groups.

(i) Minor irrigation projects - Up to 2000 hectares of are irrigated under these projects. These include wells, tubewells, ponds, pumpsets, drip irrigation, sprinklers etc. Minor irrigation projects fulfill about 62% of the demand for irrigation in India.

(ii) Medium irrigation projects - More than 2000 to 10000 hectares of area are irrigated under these projects.

(iii) Major irrigation projects - More than 10,000 hectares of area are irrigated under these projects. 38% of the need for irrigation in the country is fulfilled by the major irrigation projects.

  • Gang Canal is one of the world’s oldest and most developed canals. It was constructed in the year 1927 by Shri Ganga Singh, the then Maharaja of Bikaner. It arose from Hussaniwala, near the river Sutlej from Ferozepur.
  • The Eastern Yamuna Canal originates from the left bank of Yamuna at Hathnikund Barrage. The length of the main canal is 197 kilometres. This canal system provides irrigation facility to Hindon, Yamuna Doab's, Saharanpur, Muzaffarnagar, Meerut and Ghaziabad. After its revival, the canal started functioning in 1830 A.D. At that time, the water discharged from this canal was about 800 cusecs. In the meantime, this was increased to about 4000 cusecs.
  • The construction of Upper Ganga Canal was completed during the period of 1842 AD. Sir P.T. Cautley was the father of this project. The water was discharged for the first time on April 8, 1854, in this canal. It starts from a place called Bhimgoda in Haridwar on the right bank of the river Ganga. The length of the main canal is 298 km and the total length of this canal system is 6496 km. Irrigation facilities are being provided in Haridwar, Saharanpur, Muzaffarnagar, Meerut, Ghaziabad, Bulandshahr, Aligarh, Etah, Mathura, Firozabad, Mainpuri, and Agra districts by this canal system. Initially, this canal system was also used for waterways, in addition to irrigation. 200 cusecs of water from this canal system are provided to Delhi and about 100 cusecs water is given to Harduwaganj Thermal Power Plant.
  • The sharda Major Canal has been constructed on the right bank of river Sarda near Banbasa in Champawat district in order to provide protective irrigation facilities to the districts of Pilibhit, Bareilly, Lakhimpur Kheri, Shahjahanpur, Hardoi, Unnao, Lucknow, Barabanki, Raebareli, Pratapgarh, Sultanpur, Jaunpur, Azamgarh, Ghazipur and Prayagraj. The length of the main canal is

44.3 km and the total length of the Sharda canal system is 9961.3 km.

  • The lower Ganga canal starts from Narora (Bulandshahr). Its construction work was completed in 1878 A.D. The length of the main canal is 99.40 km. and the total length of the canal system is 8637.120 km.
  • The foundation stone of the Indira Gandhi canal project was laid by the then Home Minister Govind Ballabh Pant in March, 1958. It originates from Harike Barrage situated at the confluence of the Sutlej and Beas rivers in Punjab. It is one of the world’s largest canal projects, with a total length of 649 km.
  • The canal mainly irrigates Sri Ganganagar, Bikaner, Jodhpur and Jaisalmer districts of western Rajasthan.
  • Under the Gandak project a 739 meter long barrage was built near the Triveni Ghat on Gandak River.
  • The construction of Farakka Barrage was completed in the year 1975, with the aim of stopping the accumulation of silts in the Hooghly river. 40,000 cusecs of water from the Ganga river was diverted towards Hooghly river by a canal derived from the right bank of this barrage.
  • Ten irrigation projects have been completed on the Bharatpujha river and its tributaries in the Palakkad district of Kerala. The Mangalam irrigation project is one of them.
  • The Garland Canal system was proposed by Captain Dinshaw J. Dasthur, The whereas the idea of linking rivers was first proposed by irrigation engineer Vishweshwarya. Later, the name of K.L. Rao was added to it. The then Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee inaugurated the development plan “Hariyali”, related to water storage on January 27, 2003. Under this project, people are encouraged to conserve water in rural areas.
  • On July 1, 2015, the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sichayi Yojana (PMKSY) was approved to reduce the dependence of agriculture on monsoon and provide irrigation facilities to every farm. The Rural Development Ministry of the Government of India introduced three watershed development programmes untill April 1, 2008. These programmes are the Integrated Wastelands Development Programme, The Drought Prone Areas Programme and the Desert Development Programme. These programmes were brought under a comprehensive programme known as Integrated Watershed Management Programme.
  • The main source of irrigation in Peninsular India is Pond. Since ancient times, ponds have been used for irrigation in these areas. The land of the Peninsular region is rocky; therefore, it is not possible to construct canals and wells easily. Besides, most of the rivers of Peninsular India are seasonal, which leads to a lack of water availability for canals. In this case, ponds serve as the main means of irrigation. According to data National Compilation on Dynamic Ground Water Resources of India, 2024. Uttar Pradesh (41.15 billion cubic m.), Punjab (26.24 billion cubic m.), Madhya Pradesh (17.90 billion cubic m.) and Maharashtra (15.07 billion cubic m.) are major states of India in terms of current annual groundwater extraction available for irrigation.
  • According to the Statistical Diary Uttar Pradesh 2024 in the Uttar Pradesh (in 2022-23), in percentage of the net irrigated area by various means is Tubewell (74.1%), Canal (15.7%), Well (9.0%), Tanks, Pond and Lakes (0.6%) and by other means (0.6%).
  • Tubewell is the most widespread means of irrigation in Uttar Pradesh.

Pattiseema Lift Irrigation Project → links Godavari River to Krishna River.

Multi-Purpose River Valley Projects

8 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (8 points)

i- Narmada Valley Project:

  • The Narmada is the fifth largest river in India. In 1946, a comprehensive program was drafted for irrigation, production of electricity and flood management in the Narmada Basin. In this project, 30 Major dams, 135 medium dams and 3000 minor dams on the Narmada and its tributaries were declared to be constructed.
  • The Sardar Sarovar Project has been established on the Narmada river in Gujarat (163 Meters high near Navagam). It has an installed hydroelectric capacity of 1450 MW.
  • There are two power houses for the Sardar Sarovar Project (SSP). (i) 1200 MW River Bed Power House and (ii) 250 MW Canal Head Power House. Power benefits are shared among Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat in the ratio of 57:27:16 respectively.
  • The beneficiary states under the Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal (NWDT) water allocation for the Sardar Sarovar Project are madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Rajasthan. Medha Patkar founded 'Narmada Dharanagrast' Samiti' in February 1986 with the objective of opposing this project. In 1989, several local organizations merged and named it the “Narmada Bachao Aandolan” (N.B.A.). The Narmada Sagar Project is also known as “Indira Sagar Project”. This dam is situated near Punasa in Khandwa district (M.P.) in Narmada town. The target of irrigation of 1.69 lakh Hectares annually and 1000 MW production of electricity has been set.
  • There are several projects in the Narmada Valley, such as Tawa, Barna, Kolar, Sukta and Matiyari projects. The irrigation capacity of about 3,98,300 hectares of land has been attained through these projects.
  • 13.50 MW of electricity is produced from the Tawa project.
  • Various projects have been started at the tributaries of the river Narmada, such as the Man project at the Man river, Jobat (Shahid Chandra Shekhar Azad Sagar) project on Hathani river and Upper Veda project at the Veda river.

  • Panchet hill dam is situated 20 km south of the Maithon Dam at Damodar River. It was completed in 1959.

Chapter 49

Multi-Purpose River Valley Projects · Miscellaneous Projects

67 facts · 7 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (27 points)
  • In India, multi-purpose river valley projects, besides irrigation, also facilitates flood control, water supply, hydroelectric generation, tourism, canals etc. The first hydropower plant was established in 1897 in Darjeeling (W. Bengal) near Sidrapong.
  • Chukha Hydroelectric project was constructed with the help of India in Bhutan. Chukha dam is established at the upper part of Raidak river or Wang Chu river in Bhutan. The height of this dam is 40 meters. In 1974, construction work of this dam by the Indian government was started as a fully funded unit in which 60% is in the form of grant and 40% in the form of a loan. The loan has to be paid at the annual rate of 5% in 15 years. This project was handed over to Bhutan in 1991.It has a capacity of 336 Megawatt.
  • Bhakra Nangal Dam project is established at Satluj River. This is a combined project of Punjab, Haryana, and Rajasthan.
  • Hirakud dam project is established at Mahanadi river in Odisha. Three dams (Hirakud, Tikar Pada and Naraj) have been constructed on the lines of this project.
  • Idukki dam project has been set up at Periyar River in Kerala. Nagarjuna Sagar dam project has been established at Krishna river.
  • Telugu-Ganga Project is a joint venture of Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. This project provides water supply from the Krishna river to the city of Chennai (Tamil Nadu).
  • Mettur Project has been established at Cauvery river in Tamil Nadu.
  • West Bengal and Jharkhand both are benefitted from Mayurakshi Project.
  • Canada Dam (Massanjore dam) has been constructed at Mayurakshi river in Jharkhand under this project.
  • Baglihar Hydroelectric Power Project is established at Chenab river in Ramban district in Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Daman Ganga Irrigation Project is established at Daman Ganga River Valsad district 30 km far from Vapi in the Southern Gujarat. Girna Irrigation Project is constructed at Girna River in Nashik district in Maharashtra.
  • Pamba Irrigation Project is establishes at Pamba river in Pathanamthitta district of Kerala. Baira Siul Hydropower electric project has been established at siul river in Chamba district, of Himachal Pradesh. Suil is tributary of Ravi river.
  • Dulhasti Hydro-power Station is situated at Chenab river in Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Rajghat dam project at Betwa river in Lalitpur is known as Rani Laxmibai Sagar. Tilaiya Dam is situated at Bara kar river in Koderma district of Jharkhand.
  • Kishau Dam is being built at the Tons river (a tributary Yamuna). Tons river flows through the border of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Main beneficiary states from this project are Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Union Territory of Delhi.
  • Babli Project is a highly disputed project between Maharashtra and Telangana at Godavari River.
  • Tapovan Vishnugad Hydroelectric Project is under construction at Dhauliganga river in Chamoli district of Uttarakhand.
  • Mahakali Treaty between India and Nepal was held in February 1996. The treaty determined the limit of use of water from Mahakali or Sharda river. Sharda Barrage, Tanakpur Barrage and proposed Pancheswar Project are within the periphery of this treaty.

In 1959, there was a treaty between India and Nepal on construction of Gandak Barrage. The objective of this barrage is to provide irrigation and Power development facility in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Nepal.

  • Kalpong hydro electric power project is the first hydro electric hydroelectric power project of Andaman and Nicobar Island. It is situated at Kalpong river.
  • Rihand dam project is also known as Govind Ballav Pant Sagar Project. It was built at Rihand river at Pipri in Sonbhadra (U.P.). The length of this dam is 934.45 meter and its height is about 91.46 meters. A hydroelectric station of300 Megawatt capacity has been built below the dam in Obra. An artificial lake named Govind Ballav Pant Sagar has also been constructed under this project. It is the largest project of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Ukai dam is multi-purpose project of Gujarat 94 km far from Surat. It has been built at Tapti River in Ukai.
  • Kalagarh dam is built at Ramganga River. Its length is 715 meter and height is 128 meter. Koyna dam is built at Koyna river which is located in Maharashtra.
  • Tawa project is located at Narmada Puram district of Madhya Pradesh on Tawa river. Tawa reservoir is nestled between the western boundary of Satpura National Park and Bori Wildlife Sanctuary.
  • The Pong dam has been constructed on the Beas river Himachal Pradesh. It is also known as Beas dam. Maharana Pratap Sagar lake created by this dam was later declared a bird sanctuary.
  • Meja dam has been constructed on the Kothari river near Meja village in Bhilwara district of Rajasthan.
  • Kothari is a tributary of river Banas. This dam is mainly used for irrigation. Tulbul navigable project has been built at Jhelum river in Jammu & Kashmir.

Agriculture

Key facts from the book (57 points)
  • Agriculture plays a vital role in India's economy. 54.6% of the total workforce is engaged in agriculture and allied sector activity (Census 2011) and accounts for 18.4% of India's GVA at current prices during 2022-23.

As per the Provisional Estimates of National Income, 2023- 24 released by National Statistical Office (NSO), Ministry of Statistic & Programme Implementation, the agriculture and allied sector contributed approximately 17.7% of India's Gross Value Added (GVA) at current prices during 2023-24.

  • First Agricultural University of the country was established in 1960. Inauguration of this University (Uttar Pradesh Agricultural University) was done by Jawaharlal Nehru on 17 November 1960 in Pantnagar. Later, it was named as Govind Ballabh Pant University of Agriculture and Technology.
  • There are 15 Agro-Climate Zones in India.

  • 'History of Indian Agriculture' is written by M.S. Randhawa (Mohinder Singh Randhawa). According to standards of Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), for secure storage of food grains, relative humidity should be kept at 14%.
  • Double cropping means when two or more than two crops are grown in one crop year at one place. Intercropping is the practice of growing two or more crops in proximity.
  • Mixed farming refers to growing food and fodder crops and rearing livestock. By practicing this, farmers can increase their income.
  • Punjab is leading state in implementing ‘Contract farming’. Sikkim is a hilly state in North-East. Its maximum area is covered under forest. Less than 10% of total land is available for agriculture in this state. On the contrary, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana are the major food grain-producing states. According to Agricultural Statistics at a Glance 2024- 25, the state of Uttar Pradesh has the largest share (17.85%) in the total food grain production (2024-25) in India. As per the latest data 2022-23 (P) of the Ministry of Agriculture of India, Net Area Sown in India is 45.88%, Forest area is

23.49% and land under other practices is 30.63%. Among the top 10 rice producing countries in the world, India is the first and China is at the second place (FAO, 2024). About

37.27% of the gross area of food grain in India (2024-25) is under rice cultivation.

  • On the basis of the data of the year 2024-25, the largest Fertilizers in terms of Nutrients (N.P.&K) consumption in terms of thousand tonnes in five states respectively Uttar Pradesh (5563.82 thousand tonnes), Maharashtra (3274.17 thousand tonnes), Madhya Pradesh (3203.31 thousand tonnes), Karnataka (2325.04 thousand tonnes) and Punjab (2042.09 thousand tonnes).
  • Balanced fertilizers are used to increase production, to improve the quality of food grains and to maintain land productivity.
  • Seed village concept is a concept based on a village where a trained group of farmers are involved in production of seeds of various crops and cater to the needs of themselves and fellow farmers of the villages and farmers of the neighbouring villages in appropriate timely manner and at an affordable cost.
  • Agmark is a quality certification mark granted by the government of India under Agricultural produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937. Various steps have been taken by the Government of India for the continuous development of agriculture.
  • To increase farmers in come, the Government has promoted sustainable soil fertility through the Soil Health Card Scheme; expanded assured irrigation, improved on farm water-use efficiency and enhanced physical access to water through the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY); supported organic farming through the Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY); and taken steps to create an Integrated National Agriculture Market through e-NAM (National Agriculture Market).
  • Kisan Credit Card (K.C.C.) scheme is implemented across the country through commercial banks, small finance banks, co-operative banks and regional-rural banks.

Green Manure: Prior to the sowing of the crop seeds, some plants like sun hemp or guar are grown and then mulched by ploughing them into the soil. These green plants thus turn into green manure which helps in enriching the soil in nitrogen and phosphorus.

  • The nitrogen level available in Dhaincha is (0.42%),

0.43% in sanai and 0.34% in Guar but by sowing sun hemp or Sanayi, the land gets the maximum amount of Nitrogen 86-129 kg/Hectare. A farm gets 84-105 kg/hectare nitrogen from Dhaincha, 68-85 kg/hectare from Guar and 74-88 kg/ hectare from Lobia.

Permaculture vs chemical farming: permaculture discourages monoculture, avoids soil salinity, relies on mulching; it works even in semi-arid regions (answer 1, 2, 4).

Chapter 51

Green Revolution

23 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (23 points)
  • Norman Ernest Borlaug is the father of Green Revolution in the world. He was born on 25th March 1914 in Iowa State of America.

Wheat production has been doubled in India-Pakistan and Mexico due to a high yielding variety of seeds developed by him. Borlaug is among those seven persons in the world who got all the three awards viz. Nobel Peace Prize, 'Presidential Medal of Freedom' and Congressional Gold Medal.

  • Borlaug has been honoured with Padma-Vibhushan of India in 2006.
  • Dr. M.S. Swaminathan is widely regarded as the Father of the Green Revolution in India. Under his leadership (in collaboration with Norman Borlaug), semi dwarf high-yielding wheat varieties developed in Mexico were introduced in India and then tested adapted and multiplied for India condition, lealding to the spread of HYV seeds in India. Apart from this, special emphasis was given on the increased use of fertilizers and adequate development of irrigation facilities. In India, the programme to promote high yielding (developed) seeds was started by the Government of India with support from several international organisation and foundation, including the Rockefeller foundation.
  • First stage of Green Revolution was carried out in India from 1960s to 1970s. Its second stage was implemented in the period of 1980s. Its third stage was started in the year 1995 and covered almost all the areas of the country.
  • The most benefitted crop in production and productivity by the green revolution in India is wheat.

Before Green Revolution, the production of wheat all over India was 12.26 Million tonnes whereas in 2000-2001 it became 69.68 million tons and in 2024-25 is 117.94 million tons.

  • The increase occurred due to the increase in yield per Hectare. After wheat, the highest impact of the Green Revolution was seen on rice cultivation.
  • The main plant in the Green Revolution was the wheat of Mexican species which was brought from Borlaug’s International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT).
  • In the year, 2023-24 the production of wheat reached up to 3559 kg/Hectare.
  • High yielding variety of seeds, fertilizer, irrigation, use of technology, marketing, and industrialization of agriculture is known as Green Revolution.

On 28 July 2000, the Central Government announced a new National Agriculture Policy. Under this policy the concept of rainbow revolution was proposed. In this policy, all the revolutions directly or indirectly related to agricultural activities were included.

Various Revolutions and its Areas

Green Revolution Food production or crop production

Golden Revolution

Fruit and Vegetable production

White RevolutionMilk Production
Brown RevolutionFertilizer Production / Non

conventional Energy

Blue RevolutionFish Production
Red RevolutionMeat/Tomato Production
Black RevolutionPetroleum Production

Round Revolution

Potato Production

Yellow RevolutionOilseed Production
Pink RevolutionOnion Production/Export of Meat

'National Zero till seed cum fertilizer drill' developed by G.B. Pant University of Agriculture and Technology. This machine enables to sow directly after paddy harvest without prior seed-bed preparation.

Green Revolution (New Agricultural Strategy) → began 1966-67; first stage covered Haryana, Punjab and western Uttar Pradesh.

Chapter 52

Food Crops

29 facts · 3 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (13 points)

i. Rabi Crops

  • In India, due to ecological differences in various regions different types of cropping pattern are adopted. For example, rice and wheat in Punjab, Haryana, West U.P. etc. There are three different crop seasons in India –

Rabi Crops

Kharif Crops

Zaid Crops

  • Rabi Crops are sown in winter between October and November and harvested in summer between March and April. Major Rabi crops are - Wheat, Mustard, Potato, Gram, Pea, Lentil, Barley etc. In winter, rainfalls due to temperate western disturbances help in the production of these crops.
  • Wheat is the second most important cereal crop of India. It is produced in north and north-western regions. For the cultivation of wheat, the temperature should be between 10°C-25°C and an average annual rainfall of 50 to 75 cm evenly distributed over the growing season is required.
  • According to Economic Survey data 2024-25, the cultivation of wheat in India is done on 31.8 Million Hectare (2023-24). Some important varieties of wheat are - Sonalika, Arjun, Kundan, Amar (HW-2004), Bhawani (HW-1085), Chandrika (HPW-184), Deshratna (BR-104), Kanchan (DL-803), Gomti (K-9465) etc. For the enhancement in production of wheat in India, dwarf species has been developed for wheat by agricultural scientists. In which Lerma Rojo 64-A, Sonora-63, Sonora-64, Mayo 64 and S-227 have been examined in wheat productive states of the Country.
  • Due to the successful tests of dwarf wheat varieties, the production of wheat has been increased. Norin-10 is a gene of dwarfism in Wheat. Macaroni wheat is suitable for cultivation in dry condition or unirrigated area. Kalyan Sona (Kalyan Gold) is an advanced type of wheat varieties.
  • Yellow rust, Brown rust and Black rust are three types of rust diseases found in wheat.
  • Karnal Bunt is a fungal disease of wheat. This is caused by the smut fungus Tilletia indica Mitra. The disease was first recognized in the year 1931.
  • Tirtikale is a hybrid of wheat and rye.
  • According to 2024-25 data, Uttar Pradesh (35.65 million tonnes) is the largest producer of wheat. Madhya Pradesh (24.51 million tonnes) and Punjab (17.99 million tonnes) are placed at second and third position respectively.

Rabi crops → sown October-November (e.g. mustard, masoor); Kharif crops → sown June-July with first rains, harvested October-November. Must know

Major rice producing region are Telangana and Rayal seema which is extended on the Krishan-Godavari delta.

Key facts from the book (14 points)

i. Cotton:

  • Cotton is the one of the most important commercial crop of India. It is raw material for cotton textile industry. Cotton belongs to the Malvaceae Family. There are two major varieties of cotton found in the world. (i) Old world cotton

(ii) New world cotton

  • Cotton is an indigenous plant of India. It is also mentioned in the ancient text such as Rigveda and Manusmriti. India is the first country in the world where hybrid cotton has been developed resulting in enhanced production.
  • Black soil is most suitable for its cultivation. The temperature ranging between 25°C-35°C, 210 Frost Free day, clear sky, bright sunshine and annual rainfall of 75-100 cms are favourable conditions for its cultivation.
  • North-Western and western India are major producing regions of cotton.
  • According to data from the Economic Survey 2025-26, the three leading states in cotton production are (in 2024-25)-

1. Maharashtra 7.37 Million Bales (170 kg. of each).

2. Gujarat 7.16 Million Bales (170 kg. of each).

3. Telangana 5.79 Million Bales (170 kg. of each).

  • Maharashtra is largely covered under black soil which is most suitable soil for cotton cultivation. Cotton is known as White gold in Maharashtra.
  • Cotton cultivation in Madhya Pradesh is done on the western side of the state e.g. Plateau of Malwa and Narmada Valley. The main cotton producing district are East and West Nimar, Dhar, Dewas, Shajapur, Ujjain, Ratlam, Khandwa, Hoshangabad and Rajgarh.
  • Khandwa - Khargone region is also known as ‘white gold’ region due to the cultivation of cotton.
  • Cotton Fibers are collected from cotton seeds.

  • Pegging is a useful phenomenon in groundnut. In pegging, after fertilization, the pegs of the faded flower come out and enter the soil which grows quite close to the taproot. Once it penetrates the soil, the peg turns horizontal and continues to grow and mature into a peanut. For the cultivation of Peanut, the soil must have the enrichment of the gypsum.

It is sown in the month of October-November and harvested in the months of February-March.

The major varieties of mustard are pusa bold, Pusa, Jai kisan and Varuna. Pitambari is a species of yellow mustard (RYSK-05-02).

'Silk'

Key facts from the book (15 points)
  • India is the second largest producer of silk in the world after China.
  • Mulberry Silk, Tasar Silk, Muga Silk and Eri Silk are four types of natural Silk produced in India.
  • Chemically silk is made up of a protein secreted by cat erpillar famously known as Silkworm. These Silkworms thrives on some special plants and they develop a cocoon like protective layer around them for their survival.
  • Life cycle of Silkworm consists of four stages:-

Egg, Caterpillar, Pupa, Moth.

  • To obtain silk the silkworms are prevented from reaching the moth stage by killing the larva putting them into boiling water so as to save the Cocoon from breaking, from which the commercially important continuous fibre of Silk is obtained which is used for weaving Silk clothes.
  • According to the data released in the annual report of the Central Silk Board, 2023-24, Karnataka is the largest silk producing state in India, followed by Andhra Pradesh.

35.08% of total raw silk produced in India.

  • Assam is the major producer of Muga Silk producing a total of 65.07% of Muga silk produced in India.
  • Eri Silk is produced mostly in Assam. Assam & BTC share

56.56% of total Eri Silk production in India.

  • Tasar Silk is classified into two categories Tropical and Oak Tasar. Jharkhand produces most of India’s Tropical Tasar (2023-24) while Manipur is the major producer of Oak Tasar in India. Whereas Tasar Silk as a whole is produced mostly in Jharkhand (2023-24).

(i) Coffee

  • Coffee in India is grown under a canopy of thick natural shade in ecologically sensitive regions of the Western and Eastern Ghats. This is one of the 36 biodiversity hotspots of the world. Coffee contributes significantly to sustaining the unique bio-diversity of the region and is also responsible for the socio-economic development in the remote, hilly areas. In India, coffee is traditionally grown in the Western Ghats in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Coffee cultivation is also expanding rapidly in the nontraditional areas of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha as well as in the North East State. In India coffee was firstly grown in Chikkamagaluru district of Karnataka.
  • Arabica and Robusta are the two varieties of coffee grown in India.
  • Average annual temperature ranging between 15ºC to 18ºC and average annual precipitation of 150-250 cm is favourable for Coffee Cultivation.
  • Loamy soil or soil made from lava is perfect for coffee cultivation and it is grown on hilly slopes.
  • According to the data from coffee Board Government of India, in the Year 2024-25, Karnataka is the highest coffee producing state of India.
  • According to the figures of the year 2024-25 (Final Estimate), India produced a total of 363500 MTs of coffee, of which 256000 MTs is produced from Karnataka only.

  • Tamil Nadu stands at third place in coffee production which is 19275 MTs of total.
  • Coffee is amplified through seeds.
  • National Horticulture Board was set up by Government of India in April 1984. The National Horticluture Board is registered as an autonomous society under the Societies Registration Act 1860, with its headquarters in Gurugram(Haryana).
  • Coffee Board in India was established by Government of India under section VII of the Statute “Coffee Act, 1942”. Ministry of Commerce and Industry has administrative control of this Board.

  • Shifting cultivation is a practice in which an area of forest is cleared and cultivated by tribes and when the fertility of that area degrades the people shift to other places until its fertility has been naturally restored. It is known by different names in different regions such as Jhum in the north-eastern state, Pondu in Odisha, Kumari in Western Ghats etc.

Key facts from the book (30 points)

According to the Economic Survey 2025-26, as per data for 2024-25, total food grain production in India is estimated at a record 357.7 million tonnes.

  • According to the Final Estimates for 2024-25 in India, the production of rice is 150.2 million tonnes, production of wheat is 117.9 million tonnes, production of nutri/coarse cereals (Includes Maize, Jowar, Ragi, Bajra, Small Millets and Barley) is 63.9 million tonnes and production of pulses is 25.7 million tonne.
  • According to figures 2024-25 Uttar Pradesh is top food grain producing state with a share of 17.85% in total food grain production of the country. In this context, Madhya Pradesh (13.04%) is at second and Punjab (9.16%) is at third place.
  • National Research Centre for Banana was established by Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) on August 21, 1993. This centre works on four major thrust areas of research viz., crop improvement, crop production, post harvest management and crop protection. According to the figures of 2023-24 (Final) three leading states in the production of Banana in India are Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu respectively.
  • The botanical name of Maize is 'Zea Mays'. It is a major food crop. Due to its compatibility to diverse agro-climatic conditions, it can be sown throughout the year. At the global level, it is called as the “Queen of cereals”. Maize is used in the production of starch products such as starch powder, Dextrin, Seatex etc. Besides this, maize oil is also used for the production of Bio-Diesel.
  • Many types of alcoholic drinks such as whisky (American Alcohol), Cauim (Beer of Brazil), etc are also prepared by using maize.
  • In India, Maize is the third largest foodgrain crop in production and consumption after rice and wheat. The maturity period of maize is almost 90 to 150 days depending on season and region. The maturity period of Maize in the state of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh etc. is about 90 to 150 days.
  • According to Economic Survey 2025-26 the three leading Maize producing states 2024-25 in India are Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Bihar respectively.
  • Shaktiman-I and Shaktiman-II are genetically hybrid varieties of Maize.
  • The credit is given to Frederick Wilson to start farming of kidney bean and potato in the Bhagirathi valley. In the 19th century, he was the first man to settle permanently in the Bhagirathi Valley. He was given the nickname of Pahari and the king of Harshil.
  • According to the data of Agricultural Statistics at a glance, 2024-25 in the year 2024-25 (3rd A.E.), Uttar Pradesh is the largest producer of Potato in the country, about 58108 Thousand M.T. of the country’s total production of Potato is produced in U.P. followed by West Bengal and Bihar respectively.
  • The best variety of potatoes for processing is kufri chip Sona-2. Chipsona-3 is the best variety of potatoes for processing in plains and Kufri Him Sona is the best variety of Potatoes for processing in hilly areas.
  • The climate of lower Ganga plains contains high temperature with high humidity. Paddy and Jute crops are most suitable for this type of climate. Jute is produced in an alluvial loamy soil. In India, West Bengal is the largest producer (2024-25) of Jute & Mesta followed by Bihar and Assam. It is known as the ‘golden fibre’. Mesta is an allied bast fibre crop belonging to the genus Hibiscus (family Malvaceae). According to data 2024-25, West Bengal (0.43 million hectares) has the largest Jute & Mesta cultivated area in India.
  • In the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, Saffron is produced on a commercial level. It is also called as Zafran. The other saffron producing countries except India are Spain, Iran, Greece and Italy. Green hair desease is found in Millets.
  • For the cultivation of onion, first seeds are planted and small plants are prepared and later those plants are transplanted. As per 2024-25 (3rd A.E.) data, the onion leading three states of India are Maharashtra (44%), Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka.
  • According to the National Horticulture Board 2024-25 (Final) in India, the main mango producing states are Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka and Gujarat respectively.
  • Sindhu is a seedless variety of mango. This is the only seedless mango variety of the world.
  • Aamrapali variety of Mango was developed by the Indian Agriculture research institute Pusa in the year 1971 by hybridisation of Dashehari and Neelam varieties of Mango.
  • Lalit and Banarasi are the advance varieties of Guava. This variety of Guava is developed by Indian Institute of Horticulture Research.
  • Indian Gooseberry has medicinal significance. Kanchan, Krishna and Banarasi are improved varieties of Indian Gooseberry (Amla). Vitamin Cis abundantly found in it.
  • Stem of ginger which grows in the soil and stores food is known as the rhizome.
  • Lobia, Moong and Arhar are used as food, fodder and Pulses.
  • Groundnut, sesame and Bajra are grown in dry Agricultural regions. Irrigation of these crops totally depends on rain.
  • The main objective of National Food Security Mission is to increase the production of rice, wheat and pulses through area expansion and productivity enhancement in a sustainable manner in identified districts of the country restoring soil fertility and productivity at individual farm level; creation of employment opportunities and enhancing farm level economy (i.e., farm profits) to restore confidence among farmers.
  • India and Pakistan produce about 80% of the world total production of cluster bean. After proving the importance of Guar Gum in the extraction of Shale gas, a tremendous increase in its demand has been recorded. Guar Gum is extracted from the seeds of cluster Bean.
  • According to the data Handbook on Fisheries Statistics, 2023 released by Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandary and Dairying for the year 2022-23 the leading Inland and Marine fish producing states are-

(1) Andhra Pradesh (51.06 Lakh Tonnes) (2) West Bengal (20.45 Lakh Tonnes) (3) Karnataka (12.25 Lakh Tonnes),

(4) Odisha (10.52 Lakh Tonnes) and (5) Kerala (9.21 Lakh Tonnes). Freshwater fish production is largest produced in Andhra Pradesh.

  • Arunachal Pradesh is emerging as a major tourist destination in north-eastern India. There is a very rich biodiversity of flora and fauna. The state is famous for Green forests, wild life diversity, deep river valleys and beautiful plateau. It is home to a different variety of orchid.

Sikkim achieved the status of India’s first biological / organic state. It is notable that producing crops based on organic fertilizers completely or in other words without using pesticides or chemical fertilizers is called organic farming. Borlaug Award is given in the field of Agricultural Science. This award was started in the year 1972 after the name of Nobel Prize Winner Norman. E. Borlaug.

Chapter 64

Animal Husbandry

15 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (12 points)
  • Animal Husbandry refers to the management and care of animals for purposes such as obtaining food, fiber, labor and other products. It includes practices to improve the quality and productivity of livestock through breeding, feeding and disease control. As per 21th Livestock census total livestock population is 536.76 million in the country showing an increase of 4.8% over Livestock Census 2012. The total livestock population in Rural and Urban area is 514.11 million and 22.65 million respectively with percentage share of 95.78% for Rural and 4.22% for Urban area. The total livestock population in Rural area has increased by 4.56% and in Urban area the increase is 11.19%.

(i) Milch Breeds - The cow of this breed give more milk but the Bull are not good for agricultural work and load vehicle. It includes major breeds like Gir, Sahiwal, Sindhi, Devni, Tharpakar, etc.

(ii)Draught Breeds - It includes breeds like Nagori, Bhalavi, Hallikar, Kangayam, Khillar, Ponwar and Siri etc.

  • The country’s best indigenous cow breeds are found in Rajasthan. The cows breed found in Rajasthan are Tharparkar, Rathi, Kankrej, Sahiwal, Lal Sindhi, Gir, Nagauri, Haryanvi, Malvi and Mewati.
  • Sahiwal cow breeds is mainly found in Sindh province of Pakistan. Its milking capacity is quite high.

There are many breeds of buffalo. They mainly include Murrah, Bhadawari, Zafara badi, Suttari, Mehsana, Nagpuri, Nili Ravi, Pandharpuri etc.

  • According to Basic Animal Husbandry Statistics 2024,in India, maximum sheep are found in Telangana in 2019. The best quality of sheep breed of the country are found in the valley of Kashmir, Kullu, Chamba and Kangra.
  • Goat is known as the “Poor man's cow”. Milk, meat, leather and wool are obtained from the goats. In India, they are the main source of meat. The highest milk yielding breed of goat in India is Jamunapari. It is also considered as good for both milk and meat. It producer about 2.5-3.0 kg milk everyday.
  • According to data of Basic Animal, Husbandry Statistics 2025, the total meat production in the country is 10.50 million tonnes during 2024-25. The meat production has increased by 2.46% in 2024-25 as compared to previous year. The top 5 meat producing states are West Bengal (12.46%), Uttar Pradesh (12.20%), Maharashtra (11.57%), Andhra Pradesh (10.84%) and Telangana (10.49%).

In India, the white revolution was started in July, 1970 with the launch of operation flood-I Plan. Dr. Verghese Kurien is known as the father of the white revolution in India. White revolution is related to milk production. According to production data of Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database (FAOSTAT), India is the highest milk (Raw milk of cattle) producer i.e., rank first position in the world contributing 16.93% of global milk production in the year 2024. According to Basic Animal Husbandry Statistics 2025, total milk production in the country is 247.87 million tonnes during 2024-25. The per capita availability of milk is 485 grams per day. The average yield per animal per day for exotic crossbred is 9.05 kg/ day/Animal and for indigenous/non-descript is 3.86 kg/ day/Animal. Top 5 milk producing states are Uttar Pradesh (15.66%), Rajasthan (14.82%), Madhya Pradesh (9.12%), Gujarat (7.78%), Maharashtra (6.71%). Operation Flood was started to increase the production of milk. Its first phase was from 1970 to 80, the second phase from 1981to 85 and the third phase from 1985 to 1996. The total egg production in India during 2024-25 is 149.11 billion numbers. The top 5 egg-producing states are Andhra Pradesh (18.37%), Tamil Nadu (15.63%), Telangana (12.98%), West Bengal (10.72%) and Karnataka (6.67%).

  • In the year 1970, Indian Dairy corporation was established in Baroda (Vadodara) Gujarat. Its aim was to make Operation Flood successful. National Dairy Development Board was established in 1965. Dr. Verghese Kurien was the founder of the National Dairy Development Board and the Indian Dairy Corporation.

National Dairy Research Institute is located in Karnal, Haryana. It was given the status of Deemed University in 1989. Bihar has the highest animal density in India. In the context of total livestock in 2019, Uttar Pradesh was at the top and Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh were placed at second and third respectively. In the context of cattle stock, the top three states are West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh.

Stock farming → keeping and breeding livestock. Animal husbandry = scientific management of livestock: feeding, breeding, disease control.

Chapter 65

Mineral Resources

10 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (9 points)

(A) Rock System

  • India has fairly rich and varied mineral resources. However, these are unevenly distributed. Peninsular rock contains most of the reserves of coal, metallic minerals, mica and many other non-metallic minerals.
  • Sedimentary rocks in the western and eastern portions of the peninsula, in Gujarat and Assam have most of the petroleum deposits.
  • Rajasthan with the rock system of the peninsula, has reserves of many non-ferrous minerals.
  • The vast alluvial plains of North India are almost devoid of economic minerals. These variations exist largely because of the differences in the geological structure, processes and time evolved in the formation of minerals.
  • Vindhya Range of rocks is actually sedimentary rocks formed by the sedimentation of water suspended particles. Among these rocks, the prominent minerals are limestone, sand, china clay, etc.
  • Geologists define mineral as a “homogeneous naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure”.
  • Dharwar system is considered to be the storehouse of the metallic minerals and hence has a high economic significance. This system of rocks is rich in metallic minerals such as iron, manganese, gold, copper, etc. This system is mainly found in Aravallis, Chotanagpur plateau, Meghalaya, Tamil Nadu, etc.
  • The largest reserves of mineral resources in India are found in the Peninsular region. It is often called as the Heart-place of Indian minerals. According to annual report 2024-25, India produces as many as 95 minerals, which includes 4 fuel, 10 metallic, 23 non-metallic, 3 atomic and 55 minor minerals (including building and other materials). The total value of mineral production (excluding atomic Minor Minerals & fuel minerals) during 2024-25 has been estimated at Rs. 141061 crore, which shows an decrease of about 0.7% over that of the previous year. During 2024-25, estimated value for metallic mineral is Rs. 128261 crores or 91% of the total value and non-metallic minerals (excluding Minor Minerals) is Rs. 12800 crores or 9% of the total value. For the year 2024-25, the estimated mineral production (excluding Atomic, Fuel and Minor Minerals) would be from 20 states of which the bulk of value of mineral production of about 97.70% was confined to 8 States only. The order was Odisha with a share of 43.49% followed by Rajasthan (16.26%), Chhattisgarh (13.69), Karnataka (12.42%), Maharashtra (4.76%), Jharkhand (3.26%), Madhya Pradesh (2.78%) and Andhra Pradesh (1.04%) in the total value of mineral production. The principal mineral producing states, which have indicated an increase in the value of mineral producing during 2023-24 with respect to 2022-23 are Maharashtra (64.49%), Uttarakhand (49.8%), Bihar (26.12%), Karnataka (20.12%), Odisha (17.23%), Madhya Pradesh (16.3%), Meghalaya (15.21%), Andhra Pradesh (13.56%), Jharkhand (12.78%), Tamil Nadu (11.86%), Himachal Pradesh (9.59%), Chhattisgarh (8.55%), Assam (7.6%), Jammu and Kashmir (5.14%), Rajasthan (4.88%), Gujarat (4.33%) and Uttar Pradesh (1.7%).

Mineral Resources · Iron-Ore

18 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (10 points)
  • Iron Ores in India are majorly found in Dharwar rock system. Dharwar Rock System is economically most important rock system found in India.

Haematite and magnetite are the most important Iron Ores in India. About 79% haematite ore deposites are found in the Eastern Sector (Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha and Uttar Pradesh) while about 93% magnetite ore deposits occur in Southern Sector (Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu). Karnataka alone contributes 72% of magnetite deposits in India. Ofthese, haematite is considered to be superior because of its higher grade. Indian deposites of haematite belong to the Precambrian Iron Ore Series and the Ore is within banded iron ore formations occurring as massive, laminated, friable and also in powdery form.

  • The high-quality iron ore (Haematite and Magnetite) is explored from Bailadila Mine of Chhattisgarh. Bailadila Mine is the largest mechanized mine of India. Iron ore explored from this mine is exported to Japan from Vishakhapatnam Port.

  • Marble is a 'Minor Mineral' as defined under clause (e) of section 3 of the Mines and Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957.
  • The term "marble" is derived from the Latin word "Murmur", which in turn is said to have been coined from the Greek word "Mormorous", meaning shining stone.
  • Marble is a type of metamorphic rock that is formed from sedimentary carbonate rocks by contact metamorphism. Marble is metamorphosed from dolostone or sedimentary carbonate rocks.
  • Makrana is situated in Nagaur district in Rajasthan.
  • High-quality marble is found here. This marble is used in the Taj Mahal and Victoria Memorial (Kolkata).

Chapter 74

Energy Mineral · Coal

52 facts · 8 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (33 points)
  • Coal is solid sedimentary rock mainly constituted of hydrocarbons. Coal is mainly used as a fuel producing heat and energy. It is remains of organic matter and animal fossils accumulated in sedimentary rock by a different methods.
  • Coal occurs in rock series of two main geological ages-

(1) Gondwana (2) Tertiary

  • Gondwana coal is high quality coal with low ash content. while tertiary coal is low quality coal. Most of the coal produced in India is obtained from this region. Bituminous coal is abundantly found here. It has low sulfur content. The coalfields of India, most coalfields are related to Lower Gondwana. More than about 99% of coal deposits and production have been covered by Gondwana coal.
  • Major Coalfields of Gondwana System are - Damodar Valley Coalfield, Son Valley Coalfield, Mahanadi Valley Coalfield, Godavari Coalfield, Satpura Coalfield, Vardha Ghati Coalfield and Rajmahal Coalfield.

Map not to scale

  • Raniganj coalfield of West Bengal is situated in the upper Damodar valley which is the largest and the most important coalfield of India.
  • Coal is found in a variety of forms depending on the degree of compression and the depth and time ofburial.
  • There are four major categories of coal based on the carbon content and impurity –

(1) Peat

(2) Lignite

(3) Bituminous

(4) Anthracite

  • Carbon content in peat is less than 25%.
  • Carbon content in lignite coal is up to 25-35%. Carbon content in bituminous coal is up to 45-86%. Carbon content in anthracite coal is up to 86-97%.
  • Neyveli in Tamil Nadu is a principal lignite reserve.
  • Coal that has been buried deep and subjected to increased temperature is bituminous coal. It is the most popular coal in commercial use.
  • Anthracite is the high quality hard coal. According to the National Coal Inventory of 2025, published by Geological Survey of India based on resources estimated by CMPDI, GSI, MECL, SCCL and some private/public enterpreneurs, a maximum depth up to 1200m.; the total estimated coal reserve (resources) of India is 400.715 billion tonnes as of April 1, 2025. With continuous exploration effort in 64 coal field (45 Gondwana & 19 Tertiary Coalfield) and 15 lignite field have resulted in substantial augmentation of the geological resources of coal and lignite. As 1st April, 2025 total updated geological coal and lignite resources of the country stand at 400.715 billion tonnes and 47.37 billion tonnes respectively.
  • According to data of Ministry of coal reserves/resources (as on 1st April, 2023) are found chronologically in Odisha (100.99 Billion tonnes), Jharkhand (93.25 Billion tonnes), Chhattisgarh (85.26 Billion tonnes), West Bengal (34.39 Billion tonnes), and Madhya Pradesh (33.56 Billion tonnes).
  • The total production of coal reported in 2024-25 was 1047.523 million tonnes. Odisha is the largest coal producing state with a share of about 25.71%, followed by Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh having a contribution of 19.68% and

19.56% respectively in the national output. Next in order of share in the production were Madhya Pradesh (15.99%), Telangana (6.83%), Maharashtra (6.76%), West Bengal (3.44%) and Uttar Pradesh (1.99%).

  • The share of coking coal in the total coal (2024-25) produced in India is 6.35% and the rest 93.65% is non coking coal.
  • Major coal fields of Jharkhand are Jharia, North Karnapura, South Karnapura, Bokaro, Chandrapura, Rajmahal, Giridih, etc.
  • Jharia coalfield is situated in Dhanbad district of Jharkhand. Major coking coal deposits are situated here. It is mainly spread across the Chota Nagpur plateau, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and West Bengal.
  • Total coal production of Chhattisgarh in 2024-25 was 204.953 Million tonnes and total storage (1st April, 2023) is 85.26 Billion tonnes.
  • Korba coalfield is situated in the Hasdev river basin in Chhattisgarh.

Korba coalfield is an important coalfield of Chhattisgarh.

  • Coal reserves of Chhattisgarh are found in Tatapani Ramkola, Bisrampur, Sonhat, Jhilimili, Chirimiri, Lakhanpur, Panchbahini and Sendurgarh etc.
  • Talcher is a major coalfield of Odisha situated in the valley of the Brahmani River in Angul district. Talcher coalfield is managed by Mahanadi coalfield Limited which is a subsidiary of Coal India Limited.
  • Raniganj is a coalfield of West Bengal. Coalfields of West Bengal are Barjora, Birbhum and Darjeeling.
  • Namchik- Namphuk and Miao Bum coalfields are situated in Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Coalbed methane and shale gas are unconventional sources of energy. Coalbed methane is 90% more pure methane gas extracted from the coal seam. Shale gas is extracted from fine-grained sedimentary rocks.
  • Shale gas is not only a mixture of propane and butane but it also contains more than 90% methane, 4% ethene, 1% propane and various other gases. Huge reserves of shale gas are found in the Sindhu-Gangetic region, Assam, Gujarat, Rajasthan and the coastal region. Currently, coal industry in India is facing a lot of challenges. Some of them are low quality coal, deficiencies in coal washing establishment, higher imports of coking coal, etc.

India's first coal mine → Raniganj, on the Damodar river, mined from 1774.

Chapter 75

Energy Mineral · Petroleum and Natural Gas

37 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (55 points)
  • Petroleum or mineral oil is the next major energy source in India after coal.
  • It provides fuel for heat and lighting, lubricants for machinery and raw materials for a number of manufacturing industries.
  • Petroleum refineries act as a nodal industry for synthetic textiles, fertilizers and numerous chemical industries.
  • It is found in anticlines and fault traps of tertiary rocks in India.
  • At first, petroleum was detected near Margherita by Assam Railway and Trading Company in 1860. Next, in 1867, the first oil well was drilled in Makum (Assam). The oldest oil deposits in India are in Digboi (Assam). It is situated in the Brahmaputra Valley.
  • The four main regions of crude mineral oil are –

(1) Brahmaputra Valley

(2) Gujarat Coast

(3) Western Coast

(4) Eastern Coast

Map not to scale

Brahmaputra Valley (Upper Assam Basin) is India's oldest oil producing region,with the first commercially successful oil discovery at Digboi in 1889 and the main producing belt lies in Upper Assam, largely along/near the Noa Dihing and Dihing (Burhi Dihing) river valleys - mainly in today's Tinsukia and Dibrugarh districts and adjoining parts of the Sivasagar belt. Major oil producing centers are Nahar Katiya, Digboi, Hugri Jan-Moran, Rudra Sagar, Lakwa and Surmaghati. Nuna Mati oil refining plant is situated in Assam. It comes under the authority of Indian Oil Corporation. It was established in 1962 near Guwahati.

  • Similarly, Digboi and Numaligarh oil refineries are situated in Assam. Gujarat is placed at first in crude oil production in India during 2024-25 P (as per Annual Report of Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, 2024-25) and placed at second ifwe include offshore crude oil production.
  • Ankleshwar is extendes over about 38.98 km square area of Bharuch district of Gujarat. Here, oil was searched for in 1960 and production started in 1961.
  • Lunej oil production region is situated in the upper portions of the Gulf of Khambat in Gujarat.
  • Kalol field is situated in Ahmedabad (Gujarat). Its major producing centers include Nawagram, Dholka, Somasan, Kosamba, etc.
  • Koyali oil refinery (IOCL) is located in Gujarat.
  • The city of Jamnagar was established by Jam Rawal in 1540 in Gujarat. At that time, it was known as Nawanagar. Here the largest refineries in the world have been established by the Reliance Industries. The western offshore region is an important center of oil production in India. Under it, the Bombay High Basin is situated about 160 km from the coast of Mumbai. It wasjointly explored by Russia and India. First oil well was dug up here in 1974.
  • Aliabet Mineral Oil Field is included in the western offshore region. This oil field is situated near Aliabet Island in the Cambay Basin, about 45 km away from Bhavnagar.
  • the eastern offshore region of oil fields in India includes the deltaic regions of the Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery rivers which are highly associated with mineral oil and natural gas.
  • Narimanam and Kovilkalappal offshore regions produces crude oil in the Cauvery Basin. Deposits of crude oil have been found in the Rajasthan Desert, Bilaspur Tehsil of Rampur district (U.P.) and Jwalamukhi region of Punjab.
  • Maugalbhagyam, Shakti and Aishwarya are prominent oil-fields identified in the Barmer Sanchore basin near Barmer in Rajasthan.
  • Oil deposits in the offshore region of India is mainly controlled by the central government.
  • Most of the crude oil produced in India are from this region only.

Chapter 76

Energy Mineral · Miscellaneous : Minerals

62 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (27 points)
  • Minerals are generally found in the earth's crust in ore form. Several types of the minerals are found in a different regions of India, but these are unequally distributed.
  • Earlier, India was first in mica production. Mica was declared a minor mineral on 10 Feb, 2015, but it was classified as a major mineral after Gazette Notification S.O. 924 (E) dated 20 February, 2025. In this notification also included three other minerals (Barytes, Felspar and Quartz), which were shifted from minor to major categories. The minor minerals are Barytes (Major), Bentonite, Calcite, Corundum (Minor) & Sapphire (Major), Diaspore, Dolomite, Dunite & Pyroxenite, Feldespar (Major), Fireclay, Fuller's Earth, Granite, Gypsum (Minor) & Selenite (Major), Kaolin, Ball Clay, Other Clay & Shale, Laterite, Marble, Mica, Ochre, Other Calcareous Materials, Pyrophyllite, Quartz (Major) & Other Silica Minerals [Moulding Sand and Flint Stone (Major)], Slate, Sandstone & Other Dimension Stones, Talc, Soapstone and Steatite.
  • The only producer of asbestos as per the data of the year 2013-14 is Andhra Pradesh, whereas its largest reserves/ resources (as on April 1, 2020) are found in Rajasthan. No production of asbestos was reported in 2023-24 as well as in the previous year and no reporting mines were noted in 2023-24 as well as in the preceding year.
  • Metamorphic rock is a result of the transformation of existing rock, in a process called metamorphism.
  • Metamorphic minerals are formed under high temperature and pressure. Garnet is associated with metamorphism.

Five leading states in manganese ore production as per the figures of the year, 2023-24 (P) are

1. Madhya Pradesh 1033424 tonnes

2. Maharashtra 1032992 tonnes

3. Odisha 650856 tonnes

4. Karnataka 355057 tonnes

5. Andhra Pradesh 297537 tonnes

  • Manganese is mainly found in Balaghat and Chhindwara districts of Madhya Pradesh and, Bhandara and Nagpur districts of Maharashtra. Manganese extracted from Odisha is rich in iron content and lacks in phosphorus. Balaghat is an important district of Madhya Pradesh in the perspective of mineral resources. The major minerals found here are kyanite, manganese ore, copper etc.
  • Nickel is a lustrous, silvery-white metal. It is the fifth most common element in the Earth's crust. Nickel does not occur in a native state. The largest resources (as on April 1, 2020) of nickel in India are present in Odisha, but it is not mined. The entire demand for nickel in India is met through imports.
  • Lead mainly occurs in metamorphic rock (schist) in a combined form with silver. It is also found in Precambrian and Vindhyan limestone. Lead is resistant with respect to acidic matter and atmospheric corrosion.
  • According to data from the Indian Minerals Yearbook, 2024, Rajasthan is the only producer of lead in India. The Zawar region is famous for lead production.
  • Gypsum is found in large quantities in Churu-Bikaner-Sri Ganganagar belt. It is used for improving soil fertility. It is also used in the health and construction sectors after value addition.
  • Rajasthan is the largest (2021-22) producer of Gypsum.
  • Jaduguda Mine in eastern Singhbhum district of Jharkhand is famous for uranium production. Other uranium production regions are Domiasiat (Meghalaya), Lambapur (Andhra Pradesh), Rohail (Rajasthan) and Gogi (Karnataka). In Uttar Pradesh, uranium is found in Lalitpur. Monazite is an important ore of thorium, lanthanum, uranium and cerium. It is found in large quantities in the coastal areas of Kerala.
  • Large reserves of diamond bearing kimberlite tracts have been discovered in Payalikhand and Behradih in Gariaband district of Chhattisgarh.

21 facts · 4 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (27 points)
  • Vital energy like coal, crude oil and natural gas are used to produce thermal electrical energy in India. The National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) was established in 1975. As per the Ministry of Power, the installed power capacity in India as of December 31, 2025 was 513729.69 MW. In this, thermal energy has the highest share of 48.07%

i.e. 246941.62 MW. Coal contributes 219610.00 MW, lignite 6620.00 MW, gas 20122.42 MW and diesel 589.20 MW to thermal power installed capacity. The share of other sectors in the total power generation of India is: hydropower 50914.66 MW, nuclear power 8780.00 MW, and non conventional energy (renewable energy) 207093.41 MW.

  • Government of India is going to start an Ultra Mega Power Project based on coal with Power Finance Corporation as its nodal agency. Usage of super critical technique is proposed in this project to cut the carbon emissions. Each of these Ultra Mega Power Projects has a capacity of 4,000 MW or above.
  • Tata Power is establishing an Ultra Mega Power Project in Mundra (Gujarat). According to Ministry of Power, initially, following nine (9) numbers Ultra Mega Power Projects (UMPPs) were proposed to be set up in different states:

(i) Sasan UMPP in Madhya Pradesh - Coal pithead,

(ii) Mundra UMPP in Gujarat - Coastal,

(iii) Krishnapatnam UMPP in Andhra Pradesh - Coastal,

(iv) Tilaiya UMPP in Jharkhand - Coal pithead

(v) Akaltara UMPP in Chhattisgarh - Coal pithead,

(vi) Bedabahal UMPP in Odisha - Coal pithead,

(vii) Cheyyur UMPP in Tamil Nadu - Domestic coal based,

(viii) Girye UMPP in Maharashtra - Coastal,

(ix) Tadri UMPP in Karnataka - Coastal.

In addition to nine UMPPs originally identified a request has come from some of the state governments for installation of additional UMPPs in their states. These are given below-

(i) Two additional UMPPs in Odisha

(ii) 2nd UMPP in Gujarat

(iii) 2nd UMPP in Jharkhand - Deoghar UMPP

(iv) 2nd UMPP in Tamil Nadu

(v) UMPP in Bihar - Banka UMPP

(vi) UMPP in Uttar Pradesh

(vii) 2nd UMPP in Andhra Pradesh.

  • Neyveli Thermal Power Corporation in Tamil Nadu is the first plant of South Asia working on lignite coal. Lignite is a tertiary category of coal.
  • NTPC Farakka Thermal Power Plant is situated in Murshidabad district of West Bengal. It gets water from Farakka feeder canal and coal from Rajmahal coalfield. Ramagundam Super Thermal Power Station is situated in Telangana. Its total capacity is 2600 MW.
  • Obra Thermal Power Station was established in 1967 with the help of Russian engineers in Sonbhadra district of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Bokaro Thermal Power Plant is situated in Jharkhand.

Chapter 78

Electrical Energy · Nuclear Energy

18 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (19 points)
  • The most promising source of energy to fulfill the future demand for energy in India is nuclear energy. India’s first Nuclear Power Reactor was established at Tarapur in 1969. Tarapur Atomic Power Station was constructed initially with a boiling water reactor (BWR) that was based on American technology.
  • Production of nuclear energy requires uranium thorium and heavy water.
  • Uranium is the most widely used mineral in Atomic Power Station as a fuel.
  • A total of around 513729.69 MW of energy capacity has been installed in the country as of31 December, 2025 which includes 8780 MW from nuclear energy which is 1.71% of the total installed energy capacity.
  • Rawatbhata Atomic Power Station was established in 1973 with the cooperation of Canada in Kota.

Map not to scale

  • Narora Atomic Power Station is located in Narora, Bulandshahar District in Uttar Pradesh.
  • Kakrapar Atomic Power Station is located in Surat District of Gujarat.
  • In 1988, Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant was established with the cooperation of Russia (the then Soviet Union) in Kudankulam, Tirunelveli District of Tamil Nadu through an agreement. Under this agreement, Russia has been building two nuclear reactors for India since 2002. Under the Intergovernmental Agreement in December 2008, Russia agreed to supply four more nuclear reactors to India. All four reactors are in the implementation phase.
  • Kaiga Generating Station is a nuclear power generating station situated at Kaiga, near the river Kali, in Karnataka. It has four units.
  • The First Reactor of the Kundankulam nuclear power plant, which is located in Kundankulam area (district- Tirunelveli), of Tamil Nadu, is a pressurized water reactor.
  • Mithivirdi Nuclear Power Station was established with the cooperation of the U.S.A. The project is a part of the Indo-U.S. nuclear deal signed in 2008. In 2015, the 6000 MW project was approved by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for the coastal regulatory area. This nuclear power plant is located in the Bhavnagar district of Gujarat.
  • The Jaitapur Nuclear Power Project in India was originally associated with AREVA of France, but the French reactor business is now represented by EDF. The project is proposed at Jaitapur in Ratnagiri district, Maharashtra.

For the nuclear energy, a heavy water plant is required.

  • Thal Heavy Water Plant is located in Maharashtra.
  • Manuguru Heavy Water Plant is located in Telangana.
  • There are seven heavy water plants in the country. These are Vadodara (Gujarat), Hazira (Gujarat), Kota (Rajasthan), Thal (Maharashtra), Manuguru (Telangana), Talcher (Odisha) and Tuticorin (Tamil Nadu).
  • Nuclear Power Corporation Limited is the joint venture of NTPC and NPCIL.
  • NPCIL has a 51% stake in Nuclear Power Corporation Limited and 49% of NTPC. It was established in January 2011.

India's first nuclear power station → Tarapur (near Boisar, Thane district, Maharashtra); commercial operation from 1969.

Chapter 79

Electrical Energy · Hydroelectricity

5 facts · 0 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (75 points)
  • Hydroelectricity in India is one of the major sources of energy. Hydroelectricity is generated by fast flowing water, which is a renewable resource. It is easiest to develop hydroelectricity in mountainous areas. The first small hydro project of 130 kW. commissioned in the hills of Darjeeling in 1897 marked the development of hydropower in India. The Shivasamudram project of 4500 kW was the next to come up in the Mandya district of Karnataka in 1902, for the supply of power to the Kolar Gold Mines. Now India has a number of multi-purpose projects like the Bhakra Nangal and Damodar Valley Project etc. producing hydroelectric power. National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC) Limited is the largest hydropower development organization in India, with capabilities to undertake all the activities from conceptualization to commissioning of hydro projects. NHPC has also diversified in the field of solar and wind energy development etc.

NHPC Ltd. was incorporated in 1975 under the Companies Act, 1956. The company is mandated to plan, promote and organize an integrated and efficient development of power in all its aspects through conventional and non-conventional sources in India and abroad. NHPC is a listed company on the NSE and BSE, successfully concluding its IPO in 2009. NHPC Power Station Under Operation (Incl. JV)
