Chapter 80

Electrical Energy · Energy : Miscellaneous

24 facts · 0 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (14 points)
  • Sources of energy that appear in the form of coal, petroleum, natural gas and nuclear energy are commercial resources. Fossil Fuels such as coal, Petroleum and Natural Gas are conventional sources of energy and are non-renew able resources. In contrast, solars and wind energy, biogas, biomass/energy from agricultural residues, geothermal energy, tidal energy, and small hydropower are non-conventional (renewable) source of energy. Renewable (new) energy resources are those that are naturally replenished or restored by natural/cyclical processes within a reasonably short period of time.
  • The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy gave approval to the Consolidated Energy Policy on 26 December, 2008.
  • Solar energy is a huge resource of non-exhaustible form of energy. It is used for cooking, water purification, electricity generation, etc. India receives approximately 5 kW per cm² of solar radiation energy for nearly 300 days in a year.
  • Rampura village (Jhansi district) is the first village in India that has installed its own Solar Energy Plant and is situated in Uttar Pradesh. The first solar photovoltaic plant of 2MW capacity in India is installed in Paschim Bardhaman district of West Bengal near Asansol. Maharashtra is famous for the Satara Wind Energy Plant. The suitable states for the production of wind energy in India are Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana and Rajasthan, etc.
  • According to the figures of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy the assessment indicates a gross power potential of 695.50 GW and 1163.9 GW in the country at 120 meter and 150 meters respectively, above ground level. The installed capacity of grid-interactive wind power in the country as on December 31, 2025 is 54.51 GW.
  • According to the figures of the Ministry of New and Renew able Energy as of December 31, 2025, Gujarat (14820.94 MW) stands first the wind power installed capacity. followed by Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Maharashtra.

  • Electrical energy produced due to high and low tides in the sea is known as tidal energy. In India there are two major areas for Tidal Energy:

1. Rann of Kutch and GulfofKhambhat (previously known as Gulf of Cambay) i.e. the Gujarat coastal area. The maximum tidal range is 8-11 m, whereas the average tidal range is 6.77 m-5.23 m. There is a tidal range of height 5 m approximately, whereas the average tidal range is 2.97 m.

2. Sundarban delta in West Bengal. India’s first geothermal Electric Plant was installed in Khammam in Andhra Pradesh (now Telangana) in 2012. The geothermal energy based Manikaran Electrical Plant is situated in Kullu, Himachal Pradesh. It is famous for its hot water sources. Electricity produced from hot water sources is generated in the mountain valleys of Manikaran. Hot water sources are also found in Kasol, Kheer Ganga and Pulga in addition to Manikaran.

Chapter 81

Industry

17 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (12 points)

i. Iron and Steel Industry

  • The iron and steel industry is a basic industry. The first attempt to make iron in India started in 1830 A.D. in Porto Novo (Tamil Nadu), but this factory late failed. For the first time in India, iron was successfully produced by the Bengal Ironworks in Kulti in 1875 AD. In the year 1907, a new factory was established in India by the Tata Iron and Steel Company at Sakchi (Jamshedpur). Where raw iron was produced in the year 1908 and steel was produced in the year 1912. According to World Steel Association data (World Steel in figures), 2025, it is the world’s 10th largest (in the year, 2024) steel company (Tata in Steel Group, 2024) with an annual production capacity of 31.02 million tonnes. Map not to scale
  • Visvesvaraya Iron and Steel Ltd. (VISL) was established in the year 1923 on the bank of the Bhadravati River in Shivamogga District of Karnataka. Iron Ore is supplied from the Bababudan Hills, while limestone is sourced from Bhandigunda. Due to the lack of local supply of coal supply, charcoal or wood was used for power which was sourced from the Malnad forest area. Since 1989, it has acted as a subsidiary of the Steel Authority of India Ltd. It was completely merged with SAIL in the year 1998.
  • After the independence, during the second five-year plan of India, special emphasis was given to heavy and basic industries under which Rourkela (Odisha), Bhilai (Chhattisgarh), and Durgapur (West Bengal) steel plants were established.
  • Rourkela Steel Plant (RSP), originally set up under Hindustan Steel Limited (HSL) and now a unit of SAIL is located at Rourkela in Sundargarh district of Odisha. This factory was established in collaboration with Germany’s companies Krupp and Demag. It is situated near deposits of manganese and limestone. Iron ore is brought from Odisha's Keonjhar district. Coking Coal is sourced mainly from the Jharia and Bokaro Coalfield (including the Kargali/CCL washery area in Bokaro, Jharkhand), while Talcher coalfield (Odisha) is largely known for non-coking thermal Coal.
  • Limestone and dolomite are obtained from Birmitrapur. It gets cheap hydroelectricity from Hirakud easily.
  • The Bhilai steel plant was established with the help of the former Soviet Union in Bhilai of Durg District in the state of Chhattisgarh on the Kolkata-Mumbai railroad. The Dalli Rajhara iron ore deposit supplies iron ore to the Bhilai steel plant.
  • Hindustan Steel Limited (HSL)-Durgapur- the Durgapur steel plant was established with the collaboration of Britain near Asansol in the Paschim Bardhaman district of West Bengal. This plant obtains iron ore from the Bolani mines of the Gua area, Coal from the mines of Barakar and Jharia, manganese from Jamda (Keonjhar District) and electricity and water from the Damodar River.
  • Bokaro Steel Limited (BSL) - Bokaro -This plant was established with the collaboration of the then Soviet Union at the confluence of the Bokaro and Damodar rivers in the Bokaro district of the state of Jharkhand.
  • Major minerals required for the iron and steel industry are iron ore, coking coal, manganese, rock phosphate, dolomite and chromium etc. Due to a lack of coking coal in the country, it is imported from Australia.
  • Generally chromium and nickel are used in the making of stainless steel. Both of these are mixed with iron metal along with some quantity of carbon for the manufacturing of stainless-steel.
  • The Visakhapatnam steel plant is India’s first steel plant located on a coastline steel plant. Iron ore is supplied to this plant from Bailadila (Chhattisgarh).

Stainless steel → steel (iron + carbon) alloyed mainly with chromium and nickel (also molybdenum, silicon); chromium is the key metal added to iron. Must know

Key facts from the book (39 points)
  • Cement industry mainly depends on limestone. Due to this, the cement industry is mainly located in the areas having an abundance of limestone.
  • According to the Indian Minerals Yearbook 2022 India stands second in cement production at the global level, after China. The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce & Industry, government of India, publishes data on production and capacity of cement in its Annual Reports. As per The Annual Report 2024-25, the total installed capacity of cement plants has been placed at 640 million tonnes. During 2023-24, the production of cement was 426.29 million tonnes which showed an increase of 8.91% as compared to the year 2022-23, which reported a production of 391.40 million tonnes.

Map not to scale

  • Chunar is renowned for its cement industry. Apart from it, cement factories like Dadri (Gautam Buddha Nagar), Churk (Sonbhadra) and Dalla (Sonbhadra) are located in Uttar Pradesh.
  • Uttar Pradesh is also famous for the glass industry. Bahjoi, Naini, Firozabad, Ghaziabad, Meerut, Lucknow, Makhanpur, Hiranpur, Varanasi and Sasni etc. are major centres of the glass industry.
  • Firozabad, in the state of Uttar Pradesh is also known as the 'City of Bangles'.
  • Dalmianagar is one of the oldest and biggest industrial towns in India.
  • It is situated on the bank of the Son River in Rohtas district of Bihar.
  • It is famous for its cement industry.
  • It was founded by Ram Krishna Dalmiya of the Dalmiya Group of Industries.
  • The first Indian cotton cloth mill was established in 1818 at Fort Gloster near Kolkata, although this mill was a failure. The second cotton mill in India was established by KGN Daber in 1854 (in Mumbai) and was named the Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company. It is considered the true foundation of the modern cotton industry in India.
  • In India, cotton is mainly produced in black soils. Some of the important centers, such as Ahmedabad, Solapur, Nagpur, Coimbatore and Indore are located in the areas of large scale cotton cultivation. Thus, cotton is produced in only a few regions of India. It is equally important to note that cotton is a pure raw material, in the sense that it does not lose its weight in the process of manufacturing and the slight loss in weight is more than compensated by the use ofsizing materials. The cotton textile industry is spread all over India. Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Punjab and Madhya Pradesh etc. are prime centers of cotton textiles.
  • Tamil Nadu is a leading producer of mill-made cotton yarn in the country. The presence of numerous spinning mills, a skilled labor force, and the availability, of cheap hydroelectricity are the main factors for good production.
  • Ludhiana in Punjab is famous for the hosiery industry. It is renowned as the industrial capital of Punjab. It is known for ready-made garments, hosiery items, sewing machines and parts and machine tools.

The then Prime Minister Jawahar lal Nehru formally inaugurated the Ammonium Sulphate factory in Sindri (then Bihar now Jharkhand) on 2nd March, 1952. After that, the fertilizer plant was established in Nangal (Punjab).

Phulpur (Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh) has the largest co operative fertilizer factory.   • Hindustan Machine Tools Limited, formerly Indian Tool, is a state-owned manufacturing company incorporated as "Hindustan Machine Tools" as Bengaluru in 1953. It is a Central Public Sector Enterprise of the Government of India, under the Department of Heavy Industry, Ministry of Heavy Industries. The company manufactures tractors and watches under its watch division as well as industrial machines and tools mainly under its Praga division. It has manufacturing unit locations in Bangalore, Pinjore, Kalamassery, Hyderabad and Ajmer.
  • Hindustan Aluminium Company Ltd (HINDALCO), a metal flagship company of the Aditya Birla Group, is located in Pipari village (Renukoot) in the Sonbhadra district of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Fertilizer Corporation of India Limited is a Public Sector Undertaking in India under the administrative control of the Department of Fertilizers, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. The company was incorporated in 1961 and FCIL was reorganized in 1978. FCIL has manufacturing units in five states: namely Sindri complex (Jharkhand), Gorakhpur complex (Uttar Pradesh), Ramagundam complex (Telangana), Talcher complex (Odisha) and an uncommissioned project in Korba (Chhattisgarh).
  • The Diesel Locomotive Works (DLW) (now known as 'Banaras Locomotive Works') is located in Varanasi and was founded in 1961. The DLW is a production unit owned by Indian Railways, that manufactures diesel-electric locomotives and their spare parts.
  • Indian Telephone Industries Limited, commonly known as ITI Limited, is a state-owned manufacturer of telecommunication equipment in India. It was founded in 1948 and has six manufacturing units in Bengaluru (Karnataka), Naini, Mankapur, Raebareli (Uttar Pradesh), Palakkad (Kerala) and Srinagar (Jammu & Kashmir), which produce a range of switching, transmission, access and subscriber premises equipment. Its headquarters is in Bangalore.
  • Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) was incorporated in 1954. The manufacturing units of Bharat Electronics Limited are located in the following cities of India - Bengaluru, Chennai (Tamil Nadu), Panchkula (Haryana), Kotdwara (Uttarakhand), Ghaziabad (Uttar Pradesh), Pune, Hyderabad (Telangana) and Machilipatnam (Andhra Pradesh).

It is a joint venture company promoted by the Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL), Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC) and Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL) with an authorized capital. Chapter 84

Research Centres in India

52 facts · 7 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (150 points)
  • The first Indian Horticulture University, named Dr. Yashwant Singh Parmar University of Horticulture and Forestry, is situated in the Solan district of Himachal Pradesh. It was established on 1 December, 1985 after the name of the first Chief Minister of Himachal Pradesh.
  • The Indian Government established the "Indian Grassland and Fodder Research Institute" in the historical city of Rani Laxmibai, Jhansi. Later on, its administrative control was transferred to the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), Delhi. Considering the regional agriculture and climate, three other research centres were established in India at Avikanagar (Rajasthan), Dharwad (Karnataka) and Srinagar (J&K).
  • Indian Sugarcane Research Institute (ISRI) is located at Lucknow. It was established in 1952.
  • National Dairy Research Institute (NDRI) is located in Karnal (Haryana). It is famous for animal cloning in the world.
  • Indian Institute of Vegetable Research is located in Varanasi (Uttar Pradesh).
  • National Rice Research Institute (NRRI) was established in 1946 in Cuttack (Odisha). Dr. K Ramiah, an eminent rice breeder, was its founder and director. Subsequently, in 1966, the administrative control of the Institute was transferred to the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR). The National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) is situated in Anand (Gujarat).
  • Central Institute for Subtropical Horticulture (CISH) was started as the Central Mango Research Station on September 4, 1972 under the aegis of the Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bengaluru. Significantly, the National Centre of Organic Farming has been renamed the National Centre for Organic and Natural Farming (NCONF), Ghaziabad in, March, 2022, with five Regional Centres for Organic and Natural Farming (RCONFs) located at Ghaziabad (North Zone) and Bengaluru (South Zone), Bhubaneswar (East Zone), Nagpur (West and Central) and Imphal (North East Zone). The Central Institute for Arid Horticulture is situated at a place named Beechwal in Bikaner (Rajasthan). This institute carries out research and development work in horticultural fruits and crops.

The International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT) is a non-political, non-profit organization that conducts agricultural research for the development of Sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. The ICRISAT Centre is located in Hyderabad, Telangana.

  • Central Research Institute for Dryland Agriculture (CRIDA) is located in Patancheru, Hyderabad.
  • National Academy of Agricultural Research Management (NAARM) is located in Hyderabad.
  • National Institute of Agricultural Marketing is situated in Jaipur. National Atlas Organisation was established in the year, 1956. Prof. Shiba Prasad Chattopadhyay, was the founder director of this organisation. In 1978, its name was modified to National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation (NATMO). It works under the Department of Science and Technology. Its headquarter are located in Salt Lake (Kolkata).
  • National Museum of Natural History was established in 1978 in New Delhi. Later on, regional museum of ‘natural history’ established in different regions of the country such as Southern Region Headquarter - Mysore,

Central Region Headquarter - Bhopal,

Eastern Region Headquarter - Bhubaneswar,

Besides these, two other regional headquarters are Sawai Madhopur (Western Region) and Gangtok (North-Eastern Region).

India's first expedition to Antarctica was in 1981. In 1983, India signed the Antarctic Treaty, and constructed its first research base, Dakshin Gangotri, during the 1983-84 season. The establishment of Maitri (the second station) was done for research work in biology, earth science, glaciology, environmental science, climate, science, cold region engineering, communication, human physiology and medicine. third research centre 'Bharti', was established in 2012.

  • Central Institute of Agricultural Engineering (CIAE) is situated in Bhopal. CIAE was formally started on 15 Feb 1976 in Bhopal, with a view to providing a research platform for agricultural engineering during the 5th five-year plan. The Indian Bureau of Mines is situated in Nagpur.

Indian Bureau of Mines was established on 1st March, 1948 the recommendation of the National Mineral Policy Conference. IBM has 4 zonal offices, 13 regional offices, 2 regional ore dressing laboratories and pilot plants spread over the country. The IBM regional offices are located in Ajmer, Bengaluru, Bhubaneswar, Chennai, Dehradun, Goa, Guwahati, Gandhinagar, Hyderabad, Jabalpur, Raipur, Nagpur, Ranchi and Raipur; the pilot plants are ore dressing laboratories at Ajmer, Bengaluru and MMPL & Pilot Plant of Nagpur.

Chapter 85

Transport

33 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (28 points)

1. Road Transport

  • Since the Indus Valley civilization in India, there has been an ancient tradition of road construction. The Grand Trunk Road connected all major cities of northern India from Sonargaon (Bangladesh) to Kabul (Afghanistan).
  • The capacity of National Highways in terms of handling traffic (passenger and goods) needs to keep pace with economic growth. India has the second largest road network in the world covering about 63.45 lakh km. This comprises National Highways, Expressways, State Highways, major District Roads, other District Roads and Village Roads as under As of March 31, 2025
National Highways146204 km.
State Highways179535 km.
Other Roads6019723 km.
Total6345462 km.
  • In India, among the major modes of transport road transport remains the dominant mode both in termm of its contribution to gross value added and freight transported. As per the National Transport Development Policy Committee road transport carries about 90% of the total passenger traffic and about 67% of freight traffic.
  • The Nagpur Plan (1943) divided the roads of India into four sections.
(i) National Highways(ii) State Highways
(iii) District Roads(iv) Village Roads.
  • National Highways are the most important road systems in the country, which are being constructed and maintained by the Public Work Department and the National Highway Authority.
  • In the year 2018-19, as per the Basic Road Statistics of India till 31 March, 2019 the total length of National Highways is 132499 km. There are 668 National Highways (as of March 31, 2024) in the country.

Note: According to the Ministry of Transport and Highways (as of March 31, 2019), the longest National Highway in India is NH-27 E.W., which starts from Porbandar in the State of Gujarat, connecting Bamanbore, Morvi, Samakhiali, Radhanpur and Palanpur in the state of Gujarat, Pindwara, Udaipur, Mangarwar, Chittaurgarh, Kota and Baran in the state of Rajasthan, Shivpuri and Ganj in the State of Madhya Pradesh, Jhansi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Ayodhya, Gorakhpur, in Uttar Pradesh, Gopalganj, Pipara Kothi, Muzaffarpur, Darbhanga, Forbesganj, Araria and Purnia in the State of the Bihar, Dalkola, Islampur, Siliguri, Jalpaiguri, Mainaguri, Dhupgari, Falakata, Sonapur and Salasabari, in the State of West Bengal and Bongaigaon, Bijini, Potachar Kuchi, Nalbari, Dishpur, Nagaon, Lumding, Haflong terminating at its junction with NH-37 near Silchar in Assam. New NH-7 connects Fazilka to Mana.

  • According to the National Highway Authority of India, the highest length of National Highway (as on December 31, 2024) is found in Maharashtra (18462 km). Thereafter Uttar Pradesh (12123 km), Rajasthan (10733 km) and Madhya Pradesh (9160 km) stand in second, third and fourth place respectively. The
  • Golden Quadrilateral project of India interconnects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata. Its total length is 5846 km. Apart from this, the Highway development project connects Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Bhubaneswar, Jaipur, Kanpur, Pune, Surat, Guntur, Nellore, Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam. This project was started by the government in the year 2001.
  • The East-West Corridor connects Silchar (Assam) to Porbandar (Gujarat) and The North-South corridor connects Srinagar to Kanyakumari. They cross each other in Jhansi (Uttar Pradesh).
  • The Pradhan Mantri Bharat Jodo Pariyojana (PMBJP) is an ambitious project of the Government of India which is related to the development of highways.
  • Under this project, tourist destinations and economically important sites were linked to the four-lane road on the basis of the BOT (Build Operate Transfer).
  • Construction and maintenance of the state highway are done by the concerned State Public Works Department (PWD). These roads connect all the major towns and cities of the state.
  • According to basic road statistics for 2018-19, the states leading in state highways are - 1. Maharashtra (32,005 km), 2. Karnataka (19,473 km), 3. Gujarat (16,746 km),

4. Rajasthan (15,061 km), 5. Andhra Pradesh/Arunachal Pradesh (13,500 km). The length of the state highway in Uttar Pradesh is approximately 7427 km. The Mumbai Pune expressway is India’s first 6-lane path expressway. It starts from Kalamboli in Mumbai and travels a long journey of about 95 km to Dehu Road in Pune.

  • Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana was started on December 25, 2000. The primary objective of the PMGSY is to provide connectivity, by way of an all-weather road, to the eligible unconnected habitations in rural areas with a population of 500 persons and above in plain areas. Jawahar Tunnel passes through the Banihal pass of the Pirp Panjal range in the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir.

  • The first railway on the Indian subcontinent ran over a stretch of34km from Bombay (Mumbai) to Thane on 16th April, 1853.

In India, until 1871, the presidency towns of Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai were connected by the railways. On the basis of width, the Indian Railways routes are divided into three parts.

  • The longest railway route in India is in the state of Uttar Pradesh.

  • The headquarters of Northern Railway and West-Central railway zone are located in New Delhi and Jabalpur, respectively.

  • On 29th December 2010, Metro Railway Kolkata became the 17th zone of the Indian Railways, operated by the Ministry of Railways.
  • In India the Rail Coach Factory is located in Kapurthala. In India, the electric engine is manufactured at Chittaranjan locomotive works, a plant that was established at the Chittaranjan (West Bengal and Jharkhand) border in 1950.
  • In India the factory to manufacture diesel and electric engines was established at Banaras Locomotive Works in Varanasi in the year 1961.
  • The steam engine was manufactured by the Tata Engineering and Locomotive Company Ltd. in Jamshedpur.
  • The National Academy of Indian Railways is located in Baroda (Vadodara).
  • The Fairy Queen train consists of the world’s oldest engine. This engine was built in 1855 and was re-launched by Indian Railways in 1997. In India, the third rail coach factory is being set up in Rae Bareli (Uttar Pradesh).
  • Sal or Sakhu’s wood is very hard, heavy, strong and brown in color. It is used in the construction of railway sleepers. The Kankan Railway connect Roha (Raigad district, Maharashtra) with Thokur (near Mangaluru, Karnataka).
  • India’s first CNG train was started in January 2015 on the Rewari-Rohtak section.
  • The operation of CNG trains in India will be helpful in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and reduction in diesel consumption. For the operation of the CNG train, the railway has modified a 1400 horsepower engine into dual fuel using fumigation technology. i.e.,
  • These trains run on both CNG and diesel.
  • On 14th July 2015 Railway Minister Suresh Prabhu launched the Gandhidham-Tuna Tekra rail line in Gujarat through remote control from New Delhi. This is the first Non-Government Railway Project of Indian Railways under the NGR Policy, 2012 (PPP). The total length of this track is approximately 17 km. It will provide service to Tuna Port and Tekra’s dry bulk terminal.

In India, several railway lines have been built in the mountainous regions which are collectively known as the Mountain Railway of India. Darjeeling Himalayan railway, Nilgiri Mountain railway, Kalka-Shimla Railway and Matheran Hill Railways fall under this category. New Jalpaiguri (NJP) and Darjeeling railway stations are part of the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway. It was recognized by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1999. The site was later extended in 2005 and 2008 (to incluide the Nilgiri Mountain Railway and the Kalka-Shimla Railway).

  • Rail services in India’s northeastern states of Tripura and Mizoram have been fully initiated. In February 2013, the then Railway Minister Pawan Kumar Bansal inaugurated the first railway line in Arunachal Pradesh (Harmuti - Naharlagun).
  • In November 2014, Meghalaya was added to the country's rail map, when PM Narendra Modi flagged off the first train from Mendipathar (Meghalaya) to Guwahati.
  • Pir Panjal Railway Tunnel is located in Jammu and Kashmir (U.T.). Its length is 11.2 km.
  • Karbude Railway Tunnel is located in Ratnagiri district of Maharashtra.
  • Natuwadi Rail Tunnel is located in the state of Maharashtra.
  • Tike Rail Tunnel is located in Maharashtra. Savarde Rail Tunnel is located in Maharashtra.
  • In December 2004, the then Prime Minister of India, Manmohan Singh approved a plan to run a bullet train between Mumbai and Ahmedabad. There was an agreement with Japan in this regard.
  • On September 14, 2017, Japan’s Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and Prime Minister Narendra Modi laid the foundation of the nation’s first fast moving railway project (Bullet train project). This bullet train connects the country’s financial capital Mumbai to Ahmedabad. Its total length is 508 km.
  • The National High-Speed Rail Corporation Limited (NHSRCL) has been established to start the implementation of this project. The bullet train's maximum operating speed on this route is 320 km per hour.

Key facts from the book (40 points)

Maritime transport is a critical infrastructure for the social and economic development of a country. It influences the pace, structure and pattern of development. The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways encompasses within its fold the ports, shipping and waterways sectors which include shipbuilding and ship-repair, major ports, National Waterways and inland water transport. India has a long coastline. There are 14 major ports out of which 12 Major Port are in Operational and 200 non-major port (minor port) in the country.

  • The total coastline of India is 7516.6 km (Now- 11098.81 km) including mainlands and islands.
  • There are 12 major ports (operational) on this coast which are as follows - 1. Kolkata (Syama Prasad Mukharjee), 2. Paradip, 3. Visakhapatnam,

4. Chennai, 5. Tuticorin (V.O. Chidambarnar), 6. Kochi (Cochin), 7. New Mangalore, 8. Mormugao, 9. Mumbai,

  • 10. Jawaharlal Nehru port (Nhava Sheva), 11. Ennore (Kamarajar) and 12. Kandla (Deendayal) Port.
  • Kolkata (Shyama Prasad Mukharjee), Port is the only riverine major port in India. It provides service to two landlocked countries (Nepal and Bhutan) and the hilly states of North East, India West Bengal, Bihar, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Assam. Kolkata Port has two dock Systems.
  • The Kolkata Dock System (K.D.S) is located on the east bank of the Hooghly River and the Haldia Dock Complex (H.D.C) is located on the west bank of river Hooghly.
  • Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, India’s first Prime Minister laid the foundation stone of Paradip Port in the year 1962 near the confluence of the river Mahanadi and the Bay of Bengal in Odisha. The aim of developing this port is to reduce the congestion of Kolkata and Visakhapatnam ports. Iron ore is exported to Japan from here. In May 1974, New Mangalore Port was declared as the ninth major port of India and it was officially inaugurated in the year 1975.
  • New Mangalore Port is located in Karnataka.

Map not to scale

  • The modern port of Cochin was developed during the period 1920-41 after the efforts of Sir Robert Bristow. The first ship entered the Cochin harbour on 26th May, 1928. This port is located in the state of Kerala. A Natural Gas Terminal (LNG liquefied Natural Gas) is found here.
  • Mumbai is a natural port situated on the west coast in the country. The oldest of these three is the Prince Ghat which has been in use since 1880 A.D. Kandla (Deendayal) port is located in the Kandla Greek and is 90 km from the mouth of the Gulf of Kutch.
  • Mormugao port is located in the state of Goa at the mouth of the Zuari River. It is a major export port.
  • Kakinada port is located in Andhra Pradesh. Kakinada has two distinct port faicilities: Kakinada, Anchorage Post and Kakinada deep water port.
  • Visakhapatnam port, located in Andhra Pradesh. It is India’s deepest port. It is a natural port. Machilipatnam port is located in Andhra Pradesh. Andhra Pradesh will benefit the most from the promotion of Krishnapatnam port.
  • Chennai, located in Tamil Nadu, is India’s second largest port (first-Mumbai) and the largest artificial port. This is an open seaport. V.O. Chidambaranar port is located on the eastern coast of India in the state of Tamil Nadu.
  • Alappuzha (Alleppey) port is located in the state of Kerala. There are 8 Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) terminals in India. They are as follows: 1. Dahej (Gujarat), 2. Hazira (Gujarat),

3. Kochi (Kerala), 4. Dabhol (Maharashtra), 5. Ennore (Tamil Nadu), 6. Mundra (Gujarat), 7. Dhamra (Odisha),

  • 8. Chhara (Gujarat).
  • Shipyard is a place where ships are manufactured and repaired. Cochin Shipyard is India’s largest shipyard. In 1972, it was incorporated as a fully owned company of the Government of India. India’s largest ship recycling yard is located in Alang. Alang is located in the Bhavnagar district of Gujarat. Mundra Port is situated in the state of Gujarat. Karaikal (Puducherry) is situated on the eastern coast of India.
  • Tides are important events of the ocean that have a direct and indirect impact on humans and the components of the environment. Kandla (Deendayal) port and Diamond Harbour are tidal ports.

Chapter 88

Tourism

13 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (122 points)
  • India has always been a center of attraction for merchants, tourists and, foreigners. For the development of the tourism sectors, Indian Tourism Development Corporation (ITDC) was formed in October, 1966. The Indian Tourism Ministry popularized the idea of ‘Incredible India’ to encourage tourism in India.
  • The soul of ‘Incredible India’ is implicit in ‘Unity in Diversity’. To explore the possibilities and diversity in tourism a ‘Niche Tourism’ product promoting India as a 365 days destination and attracting tourists with specific interests was launched. Tourist arrivals in India have been facilitated by easir visa regimes such as the Visa-on-Arrival (available only to Nationals of Japan, South Korea and the UAE - UAE nationals subject to specified condition) and the e-Tourist Visa (e-Visa) facility for eligible foreign nationals.
  • Kamakhya Temple (Assam) is a prominent tourist place in India. It is an ancient temple known as Shakti Peeth of Tantrik Sadhana.
  • Besides this, Assam also has Umananda and Navagraha temples, Kaziranga, Manas Wildlife Sanctuary and Poa Mecca Mosque. Dibrugarh is famous for its oil refinery factory.
  • Haflong is a town in the north Cachar hilly district of Assam.
  • Major tourist places in Himachal Pradesh are Shimla, Manali, Parwanoo, Dalhayi, Kullu, Chamba Valley, Dharamshala. Kasauli is situated in Himachal Pradesh. Kufri is 20 km away from Shimla in Himachal Pradesh.
  • Famous tourist places in Andhra Pradesh are, Tirumala-Tirupati Venkateswara Temple, Srimallikargunam Temple of Srisailam, Kanak Durga Temple of Vijayawada, Araku Valley, Horsley Hills and Nelapattu.
  • Srisailam is a religious city situated on Nallamala Hills in Andhra Pradesh. Here temples dedicated to Mallikarjun Swami and Bhramaramba Devi are located.
  • Major geographical tourist places of Gujarat include the sea-coast of Ahmedpur, Mandvi, Chorwad, Ubharat, and Tithal, Satpura Hill, Lion Sanctuary in Gir Forest, Wild Ass Sanctuary in the Little Rann of Kachchh etc.
  • Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park is located in the Panchmahal district of Gujarat. Archaeological, historical, and cultural fossil remains of the 16th century Hindu capital of Gujarat have been collected from here. It was included in the World Heritage list in the year 2004.
  • Udvada is a town in Gujarat that is famous for its Zoroastrian Fire Temple.
  • The delightful weather of the Kashmir Valley attracts tourists at international level while Jammu is famous for the Temple of Vaishno Devi.
  • Ladakh Moon is a famous destination for tourists.
  • Gulmarg, Shivkhodi and Srinagar are famous hill station of Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Karnataka known by the name of"One State Many Worlds" is emerging as the center of tourism in South India.
  • Srirangapatnam, Mysore Fort, Nagarhole National Park, the world-famous Shravanabelagola temple, Belur, Halebid, Hampi, etc. are important tourist places in Karnataka.
  • The Biligirirangana Hills are located in southeastern Karnataka. These hills demarcate the boundary with Tamil Nadu. The temple of Lord Ranganatha (Venkatesh) is located on the peak of this hill.
  • Major tourism center of Madhya Pradesh include - Panchmarhi Hill, Bhedaghat Waterfall, Kanha National Park, Omkareshwar Temple, etc.
  • Omkareshwar temple is one of the 12 Jyotirlingas of Lord Shiva.
  • Gwalior, Mandu, Datia, Chanderi, Jabalpur, Orachha, Raisen, Sanchi, Vidisha, Udaygiri, Bhimbetka, Indore and Bhopal are important historical tourist places in Madhya Pradesh.
  • Odisha is located on the coast of the Bay of Bengal. The Surya temple (Konark) is located on the coastline of The Bay of Bengal in Odisha. King Narasimha Deva I, in the 13th century built this temple. It was included in the list of World Heritage Sites in the year 1984.
  • Major tourist attractions of Rajasthan are - Jaipur, Jodhpur, Udaipur, Bikaner, Mount Abu, Ranthambore National Park, Sariska Tiger Reserve, Keoladeo National Park in Bharatpur, Chittorgarh, Bundi, Kota, Jhalawar and Shekhawati etc. Jaipur, the capital of Rajasthan is known as the Pink City. Udaipur is known as the “City of Lakes”. The state of Tamil Nadu has a number of tourist-attracting places, including a 1076 km extended coastal region, more than 30000 temples established before Christ, Waterfalls, parks, sanctuaries, hill stations, handicrafts made of bamboo, historical places etc.
  • Point Calimere is located in the Nagapattinam district of Tamil Nadu. It is the highest land on the coromandel coast. Ooty is a famous tourist place in Tamil Nadu. Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram) is the port city of India that was developed by the Pallava dynasty in the 7th century.
  • Major tourist attractions in Uttarakhand include:

Gangotri, Yamunotri, Badrinath, Kedarnath, Haridwar, Rishikesh, Hemkund Sahib and Nanakmatta Gurudwara etc. The route to Kailash Mansarovar passes through the Kumaon region. Chakrata is located in Dehradun. Tiger Waterfall is famous here.

  • Auli is a famous hill station in Uttarakhand. The Western Ghats of Maharashtra are famous for their natural beauty. The Ajanta and Ellora Caves are famous historical sites.
  • Sabarimala temple is situated in Kerala. Sabarimala, in Malayalam, means ‘hills’.
  • Kalimpong is a hill station in the Kalimpong district of West Bengal.

Key facts from the book (21 points)
  • In 1850, the experimental Electric Telegraph started for the first time in India between Calcutta (Kolkata) and Diamond Harbour.
  • In early 1881, the Oriental Telephone Company Limited of England opened a telephone exchange in Calcutta (Kolkata), Bombay (Mumbai), Madras (Chennai) and Ahmedabad.
  • The Department of India Post started the Speed Post Service on 1 August 1986. This service provides time-bound and express delivery of letters and parcels between specified stations in India.
  • Biogas refers to a mixture of different gases produced by the breakdown of organic matter in the absence of oxygen.
  • Biogas can be produced from raw materials such as agricultural waste, manure, sewage, green waste etc. It provides both power and manure.
  • Thumba is a suburb of Thiruvananthapuram city, the capital of Kerala. Under the leadership of Dr. Vikram A Sarabhai, the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) decided to establish the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launch Station (TERLS) at Thumba in 1963. Thumba was a unique choice because of its proximity to the geomagnetic equator.
  • The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is located in Maharashtra.
  • Pokhran is situated in Jaisalmer (Rajasthan). India's first underground nuclear test was held in Pokhran.
  • The Himalayan Mountaineering Institute is in Darjeeling (West Bengal).
  • Jawaharlal Nehru Krishi Vishwa Vidyalaya is in Jabalpur (M.P.).
  • Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel University of Agriculture and Technology is in Meerut (U.P.).
  • Indira Gandhi Krishi Vishwavidyalaya was established in Raipur district of Chhattisgarh.
  • India's first nuclear reactor is 'Apsara', which started its operation in August 1956 at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in Trombay, Mumbai.
  • Moradabad is famous worldwide for brass works and glassware. Moradabad is also known by the name of Peetal Nagri.
  • Chanderi is a town of historical importance in Ashoknagar district of Madhya Pradesh. Chanderi is famous for its hand-woven sarees.
  • Banarasi silk sarees are famous worldwide. These sarees are known for their gold and silver brocade or zari, fine silk and opulent embroidery.
  • Kanjivaram silk sarees are made in Kanchipuram Tamil Nadu, so Kanchipuram is also known as the 'Varanasi of the South'.
  • Cairn (currently Capricorn Energy) is one of the world's leading oil and gas exploration and development companies. Cairn has its headquarters in Edinburgh (Scotland). The company is listed on the London Stock Exchange and is engaged in oil production in Rajasthan (India).
  • Aishbagh Stadium is located in Bhopal (M.P.).
  • Green Park Cricket Stadium is located in Kanpur (U.P.).
  • Eden Gardens (Cricket Stadium) is located in West Bengal.

Chapter 90

The Universe

26 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (38 points)

i. General Concept

  • The first rational perspective regarding the origin of the planets was probably proposed by a French naturalist ‘Comte de Buffon’ in 1749. According to the number of stars participating in the origin of planets, the scientific concepts have been divided into two parts- (1) Monistic concept and

(2) Dualistic concept.

  • Under the Monistic concept, Immanuel Kant’s Gaseous Hypothesis and Pierre-Simon Laplace’s Nebular Hypothesis became famous. Under the Dualistic concept, Chamberlin and Moulton Planetesimal Hypothesis, James Jeans and Jefferys Tidal Hypothesis, H.N. Russell and Lyttleton Binary Star Hypothesis etc. became noteworthy.
  • The latest theory regarding the origin of the universe is the Big Bang Theory.
  • Georges Lemaitre (1894-1966) was the first to present the idea of an expanding universe. Later in 1967, Robert Wagoner presented the interpretation of this theory. The Big Bang theory explains how 13.7 or
  • 13.8 billion years ago universe expanded from a very high density and high-temperature state.
  • After the explosion, the universe expanded in all directions and different galaxies of different shapes were formed. Thus, the universe comprises of an infinite number of galaxies.

It is estimated that there are appx. 100-200 billion galaxies in the universe and every galaxy is estimated to have around 100 billion stars. Our galaxy is known as an Akash Ganga or Milky Way.

  • The shape of the Galaxies varies in shape and size. Some are spiral, some are irregular and some are elliptical.
  • In 2005, the Spitzer Space Telescope gave clear evidences that our galaxy (the Milky Way) is barred spiral in shape, hence disapproving the earlier theories.
  • The universe is a collection of infinite galaxies. Every galaxy has around 100 billion stars. These stars are formed as a result of the presence of hydrogen and helium gases in their unified form (Nebulae). The gravitational force keeps the gases and dust particles in the unified form. Velocity, high temperature and organizational processes are the factors behind the formation of a star.
  • The formation of the star passes through different phases. In the first phase, a proto-star is formed after that the star enters the second phase i.e., the main sequence Star. A star of the size of our sun stays in this phase for around 9 or 10 billion years. After this phase, the fuel of the star i.e., hydrogen starts getting used up to an extent that the star enters the third phase i.e., towards its death.
  • The lifespan of any star depends upon its size. A star of the size of our sun (one solar mass) has a lifespan of around 9 or 10 billion years. The bigger the star is, the shorter is its life span. For example, a star whose surface temperature is more than 30000 Kelvin and which is 100 times the size of our sun has a life span of only a few million years. After the main sequence life of the star ends, it enters in the elderly phase.
  • In this phase, the outer layer of the star expands greatly, It becomes a Red Giant or Red Supergiant.
  • After the red Giant phase, a star witnesses an explosion in the form of a Nova or Supernova, thus entering its last stage of life. Depending upon its size it can end up in- a Black Dwarf, Neutron star or a Black Hole.

Sun like small stars – after the Red Giant phase and Nova explosion if the stellar mass is less than 1.44 solar Masses, the star will end up being a White Dwarf first and then into a Black Dwarf.

Medium sized stars - after the Red Giant Phase and Supernova explosion, if the stellar mass is between 1.44 to 3 solar masses, then a star can convert into a Neutron Star (Pulsar).

Large size stars – those which have a stellar mass more than 3 times that of our sun. These stars have the possibility to convert into a black hole after a supernova explosion.

  • In 1931 Indo-American Physicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar published his work on the Chandrasekhar Limit. The Chandrasekhar limit which is appx. 1.44 times the mass of the sun (1.4 solar mass) determines the death state of a star. Any white dwarf with less than 1.4 solar mass will remain a white dwarf forever, while a star that exceeds this mass is destined to end in life in the most violent of explosions: a supernova, creating neutron stars or black holes.
  • It is to be noted here that the Chandrasekhar limit is determined after the nova or supernova explosion of the star has taken place. Prima facie it is determined by the mass of the residue of the exploded star.
  • It is not certain that which of the main sequence stars leave a residual mass under or over 1.44 times of solar mass, after explosion. However it is estimated that stars, with 8 times the size of our sun leave a residue equal to 1.44 times of solar mass after the explosion, and stars bigger than the above ones leave a residual mass of more than 1.44 times the solar mass. The stars of the latter case have the probability of creating black holes. The high gravitational force of the black hole sucks in any left residue of the exploded star. The gravitational pull is so strong that it does not even spare passing by objects; with the passing of time the black hole gets smaller in size, until it reaches the size of a grain of sand.
  • Black hole related information was presented by Dr. S. Chandrasekhar on 11th January 1935 at Royal Astronomical Society of London. He presented the original papers regarding the subject. In the year 1983, a combined Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Dr. S. Chandrasekhar and W.A. Fowler. After a supernova explosion, the star becomes dead. Hence, a supernova is the explosion of a dying star.
  • The sun is one of the stars of our Galaxy, the Milky Way. Its distance from the Galactic center is 7.94 kiloparsecs or 25,896 thousand light years.
  • With an average speed of 720 thousand km/hour, it takes the sun approximately 22.5 to 25 crore years for one revolution of the Galaxy (Every star in the Galaxy revolves around the Galactic Center).
  • Hence the duration of the time required for the sun to orbit once around the Galactic center of the Milky Way Galaxy is known as 1 cosmic year or 1 Galactic year.
  • A light year is a unit of length in astronomy and is equivalent to the distance traveled by light in one year in vacuum (appx. speed of light in vacuum 3 × 10⁵ km/sec). Light years is the unit used to measure the distance between the stars. The distance traveled in one light year in the different units is as follows -

In metre 9.461 × 10¹⁵

In kilometre 9.461 × 10¹²

Millimetre 9.461 × 10¹⁸

Astronomical unit 63.24 × 10³

Miles 5.878 × 10¹²

  • Chandrasekhar limit is a limit exceeding which, the free revolving electrons get energized enough to leave their orbit, leaving behind the neutrons. This condition is known as a neutron star or pulsar. A group of stars that forms an imaginary outline or pattern on the celestial sphere, typically representing an animal, mythological person or creature, God, or an inanimate object is known as a constellation. A general list of 88 constellations was produced for the International Astronomical Union in 1922.
  • The Great Bear constellation is also called Ursa Major, Big Bear and Saptarishi. With the help of great bear constellation, the position of the pole star can be easily located. It is situated immediately above the North Pole of the Earth.
  • The Orion Nebula is a diffuse nebula situated in the Milky Way. It is one of the brightest nebulae and is visible to the naked eye in the night sky.
  • Proxima Centauri is the closest star to our Sun. Betelgeuse centauri (Alpha Orionis) is the second- brightest star in the constellation. It is around 700 light years from Earth. The Hubble space Telescope obtained the first direct image of a star other than the Sun: Betelgeuse. Stars revolve around the North and South celestial poles, and parallel to the celestial equator.
  • The north and south celestial poles appear directly overhead the earth’s North Pole and south pole respectively likewise the celestial equator is placed directly overhead the earth’s equator and always stays perpendicular (90°) to the poles. The celestial equator is defined to be infinitely distant. Thus, the ends of the semi-circle always intersect the horizon due east and due west. Regardless of the observer's position on earth.

  • Gases like hydrogen and helium are found in abundance on planets like Jupiter and Saturn. The Goldilocks zone is also called the habitable zone. In astronomy, the Goldilocks zone is the range of the orbits around a star within which a planetary surface can support liquid water given sufficient atmospheric pressure. Liquid water is one of the most important elements in finding life on other planets. Earth is the only known life-supporting planet in the solar system, and it lies in the Sun's Goldilocks zone. This zone is neither too hot nor too cold.

In this essay, he gave information regarding the principle of revolution. According to this essay, the Sun is at the center of the universe and earth revolves around it. Later in 1543 AD, it was been published by the name 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres).

H2 + H2 He4 + Energy

  • 7.5 minutes.

While opposite to it is on 4th July, the sun stands farthest from the earth and this position or situation is known as 'Aphelion'.

Key facts from the book (28 points)
  • The Earth is the third planet from the sun behind Mercury and Venus respectively. It is located between Venus and Mars. Survival of life is possible on our planet because of its ecology. Hence Earth has been given the name Green Planet.
  • Greek Philosopher Aristotle (384-322 B.C.) has clearly mentioned in second volume of the 14th chapter of his book "On The Heavens". But now it is universally accepted that the shape of our planet is much closer to being an oblate spheroid. Hence, the shape of our planet is called Geoid (Geoid meaning earth like).
  • Our planet Earth is tilted on its axis at an angle of 23⁰30'.
  • The Earth takes 24 hours to rotate once on its axis. This leads to the phenomena of Day and Night.
  • Basically that part of the planet which is facing the sun experiences day and the opposite side experiences night.
  • The axial tilt of 23⁰30' (now 23⁰44') as it moves around the Sun causes seasonal changes.
  • The moon is an astronomical body that orbits planet Earth and is Earth’s only permanent natural satellite.
  • On 21st March and 23rd September the Sun shines directly above the equator twice. From 21st March to 23rd September (6 months) the Sun shines between the equator and tropic of cancer. Thus, the Northern Hemisphere experiences summers and the Southern Hemisphere experiences winters.
  • On the other hand, the next 6 months i.e. from 23rd September to 21st of March the sun shines between the equator and the tropic of Capricorn. Hence, the southern hemisphere experiences summers and the northern hemisphere experiences winters.
  • Because of the slanted rays falling on the hemisphere, opposite to the one receiving direct sunlight, at any point north of the Arctic Circle or south of the Antarctic Circle there will be one period in the summer when the sun does not set, and one period in winter when the sun does not rise. For example in Northern Hemisphere the sun does not set at the North Pole and vice-versa.
  • On June 21st, the sun is directly overhead the Tropic of Cancer. This phenomenon is known as the Summer Solstice. On 22nd December, the sun is directly overhead the Tropic of Capricorn. This phenomenon is called the Winter Solstice.
  • The 45-degree latitude is often called the halfway point between the equator and the North Pole. The cosine 45 latitude equals to 0.707, hence the length of this latitude is
  • 0.707 × 40090.2857 = 28343.832 km. Therefore, the length of the 45° latitude is more than half of the length of the equator. The length of 60-degree latitude is half the length of the equator (cosine 60° = 0.5). The circumference of the equator is appx. 40090 km. Whereas the equatorial diameter of the Earth is appx. 12800 (12756 km).
  • The rotation of the Earth creates a centrifugal force which is maximum at the equator. As a result of this force, the weight of any object is minimum at the equator and increases with an increase in latitudes and is maximum at the poles.
  • The movement of the Earth in its orbit around the sun is called a revolution. It takes Earth 365.25 Days or 365 Days, 6 hours 9 minutes and
  • 9.51 seconds to complete one revolution.
  • A tropical year (also known as a solar year) is the time that the Sun takes to return to the same position in the cycles of the seasons, as seen from Earth; for example, the time from the Vernal equinox to Vernal equinox or from summer solstice to summer solstice.
  • The one tropical year is approx. 365.24 days. Normally a calendar is based on a tropical year, which is 365 days, 5 hours, 48 min. and 45.2 seconds long.

14 facts · 2 Must know

Key facts from the book (21 points)
  • The moon is an astronomical body that orbits planet Earth and is Earth’s only permanent natural satellite. The diameter of the Moon is 3,475 km.
  • The minimum and maximum distance between the Earth and Moon is 363300 km and 405500 km respectively.
  • The Moon makes a complete orbit around Earth once every 27 days, 7 hours and 43 minutes. It is the same time that is taken by the Moon to complete its one rotation. The moon is tilted on its axis, due to which its appearance (size) changes with its distance from the Earth. Because of this effect, about 59% of the Moon’s surface can actually be seen from Earth.
  • Sound requires a medium to travel. Since there is no atmosphere on the Moon, When two astronomers talk to each other it is not audible.
  • Solar eclipses occur at the new moon, when the moon comes in between the sun and the earth. In contrast, lunar eclipses occur at full moon, when the earth is in between the sun and the moon. The type and duration of a lunar eclipse depend upon the orbital tilt and alignment of the moon.
  • When the moon is closest to Earth (363300 km), then this condition is called perigee. It is during this time that high tides occur, because the gravitational pull of the moon is at its maximum. When the moon is at its farthest distance from the earth, the condition is called apogee. This is the time when low tides occur because the gravitational pull of the Moon is minimum.
  • The low tides are 20% smaller than the high tides.
  • A lunar perigee occurred on December 22nd, 1999 due to which the moon appeared to be the brightest. Again on November 14th, 2016 a full perigee occurred due to which the moon for the first time in over 60 years appeared to be the largest and the brightest. In common language, this phenomenon is known as supermoon. A supermoon occurs when the full moon coincides with the moon's orbit being closest (perigee) to Earth.
  • During a supermoon, the moon appears roughly 14%, larger in diameter and 30% brighter.
  • During a total lunar eclipse, earth completely blocks direct sunlight from reaching the moon. The only light reflected from the lunar surface has been refracted by Earth’s Atmosphere. Due to the reddish colour, a totally eclipsed moon is sometimes called a blood moon.
  • A Blue Moon is an additional full moon that appears in a subdivision of a year-either as the third or fourth full moon in a season or a second full moon in a month of the common calendar. One lunar month is around 29.5 days long. Ifwe multiply 29.5 days by 12 months we get 354 days, which means there could be 12 full moons in a year. Since 11 days are still left in a year, approximately every 2.7154 years the condition for a Blue moon (one extra full moon) comes into existence. In every 2.7154 years there would be a month that has two full moons, however the difference between these two full moons will always be 29.5 days. Traditionally the second full moon of the month is called a Blue Moon.
  • Accordingly in the year 2009 there were two full moons in December, one on 2nd December and one on 31st December. The one that occurred on 31st December was called a Blue Moon.
  • According to the new definition of the Almanac the Blue Moon phenomenon is the occurrence of one extra full moon in an astronomical season. There are four astronomical seasons in a year- starting from 21st March to 23rd September (the Equinoxes) and the other two starting from 21st June to 22nd December (summer and winter solstice respectively). Hence the astronomical seasons are like this –

1st Astronomical season (21st March to 20th June)

2nd Astronomical season (21st June to 22nd September) 3rd Astronomical season (23rd September to 21st December) 4th Astronomical season (22nd December to 20th March) Every season is divided into 3 months. Hence every season will normally have 3 full moons, however in every 2.7154 years, one of the above 4 seasons will have 4 full moons instead of3. The astronomical season that has the 4th full moon will be known as the season with the Blue Moon. It is to be noted however that the 3rd full moon will be considered as the Blue moon and not the 4th one. It is because only then will the names of the other full moons, such as the moon before the solstice and the Moon after the solstice, fall at the proper times relative to the solstices and equinoxes. Hence, according to the above definition, the year 2010 witnessed 4 full moons the astronomical season starting from 23rd September to 22nd December. 25th September, 24th October, 21st November and 20th December witnessed full moons. The full moon of21st November 2010 was referred to as a Blue Moon.

  • The weight of any body on a planet or satellite depends upon the mass of the body and the gravitational acceleration of the planet. (Weight = mass × gravitational acceleration). The gravitational acceleration on the moon is 1/6th of that of planet Earth. Hence, any body or object taken to the moon has its weight reduced to 1/6th of its weight on planet Earth. The area of the large black patch as seen from the Earth is called Lunar Mare or Sea of Tranquility. It was the landing site for the first crewed landing on the Moon on July 20, 1969. Astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin Buzz Aldrin Junior made a smooth touchdown in the Apollo 11 Lunar Module named Eagle. The third astronaut on this mission was Michael Collins, however, he did not step on the Moon.
  • The Apollo 11 returned to Earth and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on July 24, 1969. The mission brought back substances from the surface of the Moon which weighed around 47 pounds. It was used for research purposes.
  • Chandrayaan-1 was India’s first lunar probe. It was launched by the Indian Space Research Organisation on 22 October, 2008 and operated until August 2009. India launched the space craft using a PSLV-XL rocket (PSLV-C11). The vehicle was inserted into lunar orbit on 8 November 2008.
  • The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) set up a Indian Deep Space Network (IDSN) centre in Byalalu (Bengaluru) to track Chandrayaan-1.
  • Chandrayaan-2 is India’s second lunar exploration mission after Chandrayaan-1 developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation, the mission was launched to the Moon by a Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mk III - M1 (GSLV-MkIII-M1) on July 22, 2019. Chandrayaan-3 mission took off on July 14, 2023 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Andhra Pradesh. On August 5, 2023 the mission entered lunar orbit. On August 17, the lander module separated from the propulsion module. The first and second deboosting occurred on August 18 and 20 respectively. OnAugust 23, 2023 the lander landed on the south pole of the Moon. India's third lunar mission, Chandrayaan - 3 made history in August, 2023 by successfully achieving a soft landing on the south pole of the Moon.

With this, India became the first nation to land on the Moon's south pole and the fourth (after Russia, U.S.A. and China) to land successfully on Earth's only natural satellite.

Between 16 and 22 July 1994, the comet collided with Jupiter, providing the first direct observation of an extraterrestrial collision of solar system objects. However, Jupiter was not harmed by this collision.

i. Latitudes

  • Latitude is the angular distance of a point on the earth’s surface, measured in degrees from the center of the earth.
  • It is parallel to the line of the equator, which lies midway between the poles.
  • The latitude angle is denoted by the Greek lowercase letter Phi (). 0° latitude is also known as the equator. It is halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole. The equator thus divides the planet into the Northern and Southern hemisphere.
  • The earth is widest at the equator. All other latitudes are smaller than the equator.
  • The North Pole has a latitude of 90°N and the South Pole has a latitude of 90°S. In each hemisphere, latitudes are counted from 0° to the poles. Hence, altogether there are 179 latitudes (including the equator). Besides this, there are 179 real circle latitudes as the 90° N and 90°S latitudes are points on the earth’s surface.
  • The 23.5° N latitude in the Northern Hemisphere is known as the Tropic of Cancer whereas the 66.5° N latitude in the Northern Hemisphere is known as Arctic Circle.
  • Similarly, the 23.5°S latitude in the southern Hemisphere is known as the Tropic of Capricorn and 66.5° south latitude in the Southern Hemisphere is known as the Antarctic Circle.
  • The 0° latitude (equator) and 0° longitude (Prime Meridian) intersect each other in the Gulf of Guinea located on the western coast of Africa. The Gulf is located in the Atlantic Ocean. The north and south of any place on a globe or a map is determined by latitudes. The latitudinal value in degrees of any place is directly proportional to its extent in the north of the equator for example - Beijing (China) - 39°55'N, New Delhi - 28°38'N, New York (USA) - 40°45' N and Rome (Italy) - 41°54' N. Hence among these Rome is the most northern city.

Latitude is only North or South of the Equator and ends at the Poles (ninety degrees). So 'forty-five degrees South' is valid; East/West values are longitudes.

Chapter 104

The Earth · The Longitude

25 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (13 points)
  • Longitudes are imaginary lines joining the North and South Poles. They are also known as Meridians of Longitude or Lines of Longitude.
  • By convention, one of the longitudes was called the Prime Meridian. The longitudes of other places are measured as the angle east or west from the Prime Meridian, ranging from 0° at the Prime Meridian, to 180° eastward and 180° westward. In 1884, at the International Meridian Conference in Washington, D.C., 22 countries voted to adopt the Greenwich meridian as the Prime Meridian of the world. The 180th Meridian or Antemeridian is the meridian 180° both east and west of the Prime Meridian. Thus, it is common to both east longitude and west longitude. Hence there are 360 longitudes.
  • Since Earth makes one complete rotation of 360° in one day or 24 hours, it passes through 15° in one hour or 1° in 4 minutes. The Earth rotates from west to east, so every 15° we go eastward local time is advanced by 1 hour.
  • The International Date Line, established in 1884 passes through the Mid-Pacific Ocean and roughly follows a 180° longitude North-South line on the Earth. It is located halfway around the world from the prime meridian.
  • When we cross the International Date Line from west to east, there is a decrease of one day and if you cross the line from east to west there is a gain of an extra day. This is because there is a difference of 24 hours between 180°E and 180°W longitude. 180°E and 180°W longitude are the same and written as only 180°.
  • The time at 180°E is 12 hours ahead and at 180° W it is 12 hours behind Greenwich time. A time zone is a region or area that observes the same standard time. The 360 longitudes have been divided into 24 time zones. The world is divided longitudinally into time zones, with each hour difference roughly 15° apart. This means that every time zone has a difference of 1 hour and every longitude has a difference of 4 minutes.
  • The international standard time is determined by the prime meridian.
  • In the Northern Hemisphere the Prime Meridian passes through the United Kingdom, France and Spain in Europe and Algeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Togo and Ghana in Africa. The only landmass crossed by the Meridian in the Southern Hemisphere is Antarctica.
  • Apart from the United Kingdom there are a few more countries that despite being away from GMT (Greenwich Mean Time), use it for determining their standard time. These countries/areas are – Iceland, Ireland, Portugal, Western Sahara, Sao Tome Mauritania, Mali, Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Ghana, Liberia, Cote d'Ivoire, Burkina Faso, Gambia, Saint Helena etc. The time difference between Indian Standard Time (82°30' E longitude) and GMT is 5.30 hours.
  • Katchal, a tiny island near Nicobar Island was virtually unknown untill the Royal Greenwich Laboratory declared that it would be the first inhabited place on Earth to catch the rays of the first sunrise of the millennium. The Katchal island is located at a distance of 1600 km from the mainland of India and 418 km from Port Blair port. The island is located at 7°56' North latitude and 93° 24' East longitude.
  • International Date Line (IDL) is an imaginary line of demarcation on the surface of the Earth that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole and demarcates the change of one calendar day to the next.
  • IDL is roughly based on the meridian of 180° longitude, roughly down the middle of the Pacific Ocean and halfway around the world from the Greenwich Meridian. The IDL is deviated east or west away from the meridian eight places to prevent any anomalies regarding the date at a particular place.
  • The difference between the International Date Line (180° longitude) and Indian Standard Time (82°30' East) is 97°30' longitude. International Date Line passes through the Bering Strait (Pacific Ocean).

Cairo, 2 hours ahead of Greenwich → about 30° E longitude (1° = 4 minutes; 120 minutes ÷ 4 = 30°).

Chapter 108

The Earth · Day & Night

9 facts · 3 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (13 points)
  • The earth has two kinds of movements – (1) Rotation i.e. rotation of Earth around its own axis. (2) Revolution i.e. the movement of the earth around the sun.
  • The earth on its axis rotates from west to east. The rotation of the earth causes the phenomena of Day and Night. The earth is tilted on its axis at an angle of 23.5° as a result of which the duration of Day and Night is not always equal.
  • However, the duration of Day and Night is always equal on the equator as the sun always shines vertically overhead on the equator.
  • Between 21st March and 23rd September the sun shines between the equator and the Tropic of Cancer, as a result of which the Northern Hemisphere receives more than 12 hours of sunlight. Thus the Days are longer and nights are shorter in the Northern Hemisphere during this time.
  • Similarly, from 23rd September to 21st March, the sun shines between the Equator and the Tropic of Capricorn. As a result the Southern Hemisphere receives more than 12 hours of sunlight. As one moves closer to the South Pole the duration of Day keeps on increasing, during this period the South Pole witnesses a 6 month long daytime.
  • Earth revolves around the sun in an elliptical orbit and completes one revolution around the sun in approx 365 days and 6 hours. Thus because of revolution and axial tilt, the angle of insolation changes throughout the year. Solstices occur twice a year.
  • Summer solstice – On 20/21st June the sun shines vertically overhead at Tropic of Cancer. This phenomenon is called the summer solstice. On 20/21st June the Northern Hemisphere experiences the lengthiest day. The phenomenon is also called June solstice. During this time the Southern Hemisphere witnesses the shortest day.
  • Winter solstice – On 21/22nd December, the sun shines vertically overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn. This phenomenon is called the winter solstice. During this time the Southern Hemisphere witnesses the lengthiest day and Northern Hemisphere witnesses the shortest day. This phenomenon is also known as the December solstice.
  • On 20/21st March The Vernal Equinox occurs and on 22/23rd September The Autumnal Equinox. During this time the length of day and night is equal. Due to the revolution and axial tilt of the Earth, the Tropic of Cancer (23.5° North Latitude) in the Northern Hemisphere starts getting oriented towards the sun from 21 March and by 21st June the sun is vertically overhead the Tropic of Cancer.
  • The size of the shadow of any object depends upon the size of the object, the distance from the sun and the angle it creates with respect to the rays of the sun.
  • The size of the shadow will be the smallest when the angle is least.
  • When the angle created is 0° there will be no shadow formation.
  • The shadow formation in the Northern Hemisphere will be at a minimum on 21st June.

Equal day and night → equinoxes: 20/21 March and 22/23 September, when the Sun is overhead at the Equator. Must know

Chapter 109

The Earth · Origin of the Earth

2 facts · 0 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (11 points)
  • Earth is one of the planets in the solar system. Its origin is not different from that of the other planets. Different scholars have propounded different theories regarding the subject.
  • One of the earliest works on the subject was presented by Immanuel Kant. He propounded the theory of nebulous material.
  • In 1755 A.D. Immanuel Kant presented the Gaseous hypothesis. Later in 1796 A.D., Laplace presented his research on the topic which came to be known as Nebular Hypothesis. In 1905 A.D. Chamberlin and Moulton proposed the Chamberlin-Moulton planetesimal hypothesis to describe the formation of the solar system. The theory was based on the idea that a star passed close enough to the sun early in its life to cause tidal bulges to form on its surface, causing the material to be ejected repeatedly from the sun. Due to the gravitational effects of the passing star, materials would cool and condense into numerous small bodies, which they called planets.
  • In 1919 the famous British scientist James Jeans propounded the Tidal Hypothesis and another scientist Sir Harold Jeffreys made some corrections to it. After some years, the theory of a wandering star around the sun started getting acceptance. The theory was called Binary Theories.
  • In 1943, Otto Schmidt propounded the interstellar dust hypothesis. He proposed that the sun, in its present form, passed through a dense interstellar cloud and emerged enveloped in a cloud of dust and gas. Otto Schmidt of Russia and Carl Weizsacker of Germany revised the Nebular Hypothesis.

They believed dust like ‘Solar Nebula’ with heavy helium and hydrogen surrounds the sun. A disk-shaped cloud was created by the friction of particles in the solar Nebula. The planet was formed due to the accretion process.

  • In modern times the most accepted theory regarding the origin of Universe is the Big Bang Theory also known as expanding Universe Theory. Universal expansion was proved by Edwin Hubble in 1920. According to the Big Bang Theory, a violent explosion of a tiny body occurred which resulted in huge expansion and the change of some particles into an energy form. Due to this expansion, some energy got converted into matter. This happened 13.7/13.8 billion years ago.
  • Another proof of this Edwin Hubble concluded that galaxies are drifting apart. This is important observational evidence consistent with the hypothesis of an expanding Universe. After initial expansion, the universe cooled sufficiently to allow the formation of subatomic particles and later simple atoms. Giant clouds of these elements later combined due to gravity eventually forming early stars and galaxies. The galaxies further broke down resulting in the formation of stars and stars broke down (ran out of fuel) resulting in the formation of early planets.
  • In 1907 John Joly, used his knowledge of mineralogy to figure out the age of different minerals. According to him certain rock-forming minerals were often characterized by the presence of small circular dark spots or concentric rings. He called it the Mineral Halo.
  • Professor H.H. Russell used Uranium –Lead and Thorium-Lead to determine the age of Earth. According to it the age of our planet is 2 billion and 25 crore years and 4 billion and 60 crore year old respectively.
  • Radiometric dating has proven to be the most successful way offiguring out the Earth’s age. As Uranium and Thorium are found in one form or the other in different quantities in every rock formation, the Uranium Dating Technique to determine the age of Earth becomes very useful.

Gas and dust (interstellar dust) hypothesis of Earth's origin → Otto Schmidt. Tidal → James Jeans, Harold Jeffreys. Nova → F. Hoyle, Littleton.

Chapter 110

The Earth · The Geological History

19 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (26 points)
  • Geological History of Earth follows the major events in Earth’s past based on the geological time scale. The first efforts to understand the Geological History of Earth were made by a French naturalist Comte de Buffon. At present the geological time scale is used, which is a system of chronological dating that relates geological states to time.
  • The primary defined divisions of time are eons. Eons are divided into eras which are in turn divided into periods and epochs.
  • Pre Cambrian Era – Earth was initially molten due to extreme volcanism and frequent collisions with other bodies. Water began accumulating in the atmosphere. The only flora present at this time was seagrasses. In the warm oceans emergence of spineless creatures also took place.

A geological period is one of the several subdivisions of geological time. Every period is named after its characteristic events.

(1) Cambrian Period – The waters of the Cambrian period appear to have been widespread and shallow. The seas saw the emergence of creatures with spinal cord along with spinal cord during this period.

(2) Ordovician Period – By this time process of mountain formation had started and thus period witnessed heavy volcanic activity. Flora and fauna were only limited to the seas.

(3) Silurian Period – The period witnessed the emergence of terrestrial flora however leaf formation was yet not present. Diversity in the species of flora was also seen. A very prominent phenomenon of this period was large scale development and expansion of coral reefs.

(4) Devonian Period - The period was a time of great tectonic activity as a result of which it witnessed large scale mountain formations and volcanic activities. Various varieties of Fish emerged and evolved during this period, hence the period is also known as the ‘Age of Fishes’.

(5) Carboniferous period – Our Earth is made up of different plates. These plates are not stationary but keep moving because of tectonic activity. Hence, these plates are responsible for shifting of the continents and oceanic floors into various parts of the planet. The Carboniferous was a time of active mountain building, as the supercontinent Pangea came together. The supercontinent was surrounded by a large water body. The sea was named Panthalassa by Wegener. The northern part of Pangea i.e. Laurasia (North America, Europe and Asia) and southern part Gondwana (South America, Africa, Madagascar, Peninsular India, Australia and Antarctica).

(6) Permian Period – During this period, because of geological turmoil, the birth of high mountain ranges was seen in Europe, Asia and Eastern United States of America (Appalachian). Another factor witnessed was the increase in terrestrial species.

(7) Triassic Period – The period witnessed the emergence of carnivorous aquatic reptiles that had a resemblance to and characteristics of fishes. The period also witnessed the first evolution of terrestrial mammals. Flies and termites also came into the picture during this period along with the origin of dinosaurs.

(8) Jurassic Period – This period saw the development of the size and diversity of terrestrial reptiles. Some aerial birds such as Archaeopteryx also emerged during this period. This period was dominated by dinosaurs.

Archaeological evidence of dinosaurs in India has been found at Raiyoli in Mahisagar district of Gujarat and in Bara Simla Hills near the rivers Narmada in Jabalpur district of Madhya Pradesh.

(9) Cretaceous Period – Geological developments and transformations were very active during this period. As a result the Rocky Mountains, Andes Mountain ranges of Europe and Isthmus of Panama were formed.

The tertiary period has been categorized into different epochs. They are as follows -

(1) Palaeocene Epoch

(2) Eocene Epoch – The epoch saw the formation of the Indian Ocean, Atlantic Ocean and the Himalayan orogeny.

(3) Oligocene Epoch - The epoch witnessed expansion of land mass. Geological activity continued in Europe and America and the formation of Alps started.

(4) Miocene Epoch – The epoch witnessed a lot of geological activity as a result of which Alps mountain range was formed, there was an uplift in the height of the lesser Himalayas and Greater Himalayas.

(5) Pliocene Epoch – The North Sea, Black Sea, Arabian Sea and Caspian Sea were formed the formation of the Shiwalik range also took place during this epochs.

Quaternary Period - has been divided into two Epochs Pleistocene Epoch and Holocene Epochs.

Pleistocene Epoch - The Pleistocene Epoch is defined as the time period that began nearly 2.0 million years ago and lasted until about 10,000 years ago. The most recent ice age occurred then. Almost all the continents experienced glacier formation. The ice-sheets spread was categorized into four different times. Hence, sub-ice ages have been classified and named according to their area of occurrence. They are as follows –

Nebraskan, Kansan Illinois, Iowa and Wisconsin in North America. Similarly, Albrecht Penck and Eduard Bruckner classified the ice ages of Europe. They are as follows – Gunz, Mindel, Riss, Wurm.

  • Holocene Epoch – The Holocene Epoch began 10,000 years ago.
  • The melting of ice sheet led to reemergence and expansion of forests in Europe. Aquatic flora and fauna evolved into their present biological characteristics.
  • The period between 1300 to 1870 A.D. is known as the Little Ice Age. During this time Europe and North America were much colder as compared to the 20th century.

'Great Ice Age' → Pleistocene Epoch, from about 2 million to about ten thousand years ago.
