Chapter 111

Rocks

10 facts · 0 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (27 points)

The Earth's crust is made up of rocks. A rock is a naturally occurring solid aggregate of one or more minerals or mineraloids, and it may also contain glass rock fragments, fossils, or organic matter such as plant material in coal. Petrology is the study of rocks, which is an essential component of geology.

  • The major groups of rocks are defined as igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.

Igneous Rocks – Igneous rock is formed through the cool ing and solidification of magma or lava. They are granular in texture and are not found in the stratified form. They are devoid of any kind of fossils. Igneous rocks often have a correlation with volcanic activities. Igneous rocks are hard for water to penetrate. Igneous rock is found both in crystalline and non-crystalline form. They are also known as primary rocks. Igneous rocks are divided into two main categories-

(a) Plutonic or intrusive rocks – formed when magma cools and crystallises slowly within the earth’s crust. Ex.-granite, gabbros and pegmatite.

(b) Volcanic or extrusive rocks are – Basalt, volcanic breccias etc.

Sedimentary rocks – Sedimentary rocks are formed at the Earth’s surface by the accumulation and cementation of fragments of earlier rocks, minerals and organisms or as chemical precipitates and organic growth in water (sedimentation).

  • Sediments are formed by the weathering of earlier rocks (igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic) by erosion from a source and are then transported to the place of deposition by water, wind, ice and mass movement of glaciers (agents of denudation). After this through the process of lithification, loose, unconsolidated sediments are turned into solid sedimentary rocks.
  • Many sedimentary rocks are able to retain their specific characteristics in their depository layer, even after lithification. It is the reason why sand stones have multiple layers of different concentrations.
  • Sedimentary rocks are formed by the accumulation of sediments. There are three basic types of sedimentary rocks-

(i) Sedimentary rocks formed as a result of mechanical processes- Ex - sandstones, shale, conglomerate etc.

(ii) sedimentary rocks - limestone, coal, etc.

(iii) Chemical sedimentary rocks - halite, potassium and magnesium salt etc.

Metamorphic Rocks – These rocks are formed by subjecting any rock type – sedimentary rock or igneous rock to different temperature and pressure conditions and chemical processes than those in which the original rock was formed. This process is called metamorphism meaning “change of form”. The result is a profound change in physical properties and chemistry of the stone. The temperature and pressure required for this process are always higher than those found at the Earth’s surface.

Metamorphosed form of Igneous Rocks –

(1) Granite – Gneiss

(2) Basalt – Schist

(3) Basalt – Amphibolite

Metamorphosed form of Sedimentary Rocks -

(1) Shale – Slate

(2) Limestone – Marble

(3) Chalk and Dolomite – Marble

(4) Sandstone – Quartzite

(5) Conglomerate - Gneiss

Metamorphosed form of Metamorphic Rocks –

(1) Slate – Phyllite

(2) Phyllite – Schist

(3) Gabbro – Serpentine

Igneous rock → cooling and solidification of magma/lava. Extrusive (on the surface, e.g. basalt); intrusive (inside the crust, e.g. granite).

The Volcano

Key facts from the book (17 points)
  • A volcano is a rupture in the crust of a planetary mass object, such as Earth, that allows hot lava, volcanic ash and gases to escape from a magma chamber below the surface.
  • Among the gases emitted through a volcanic eruption the, highest quantity is that of water vapor (H₂O). Other gases emitted are carbon-dioxide (CO₂), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), hydrogen (H₂), carbon-monoxide (CO), hydrogen chloride (HCl), hydrogen fluoride (HF) and helium (He). Magma is made of molten rock and is stored in the Earth’s interior. lava is magma that reaches the Earth's surface with temperature ranging from about 600°C 1200°C. When Lava reaches the surface it cools to form igneous rocks. The composition of almost all lava of the earth’s crust is dominated by silica (SiO₂) materials. Based on the silicate, lava can be classified into two types- Acidic Lava and Basic Lava.
  • Acidic lava is highly dense and sticky in nature and has high silica content. Basic lava, on the other hand is less dense and has low silica content.
  • Intrusive igneous rocks are formed when lava cools and solidifies before reaching the earth’s surface. Igneous rocks are of two types – intrusive and extrusive.
  • Caldera is an extended version of a volcanic vent.
  • A geyser is a spring characterized by intermittent discharge of water ejected turbulently and accompanied by steam. Generally, all Geyser field sites are located near the active volcanic areas, and the geyser effect is due to the proximity of magma. For example the Old Faithful Geyser of Yellowstone National Park in the United States of America.
  • A fumarole is the last phase in a volcanic activity. It is an opening that emits steam and gases. The name solfatara is given to fumarole that emit sulfurous gases. Mount Katmai of Alaska (USA) is known as the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes. Volcanoes are categorized according to their level of activeness–

(1) Active Volcano – An active volcano has its vent open and keeps emitting smoke, gas and lava often. At present Mount Kilauea is the one of the world's most active volcano. Situated on Hawaiian Islands of the USA it has been in an active state from between 1983 to 2018.

  • The top three most active volcanoes are – Kilauea, Mount Etna and Piton de la Fournaise.
  • On the basis of size, the largest active volcano on Earth is Mauna Loa, situated on Hawaiian Islands. Mount Etna is an active volcano on the east coast of the island of Sicily in Italy. It stands 3357 meters tall.
  • Stromboli is an active volcano on Stromboli Island, north of Sicily in the Tyrrhenian Sea. The volcano has erupted many times and is constantly active with minor eruptions, often visible from many points on the island and from the surrounding sea, giving rise to Island’s nickname “Lighthouse of the Mediterranean.”
  • Nevados Ojos del Salado is an active volcano in the Andes on the Argentina Chile border and the highest active volcano in the world at 6879 m.
  • Mount Erebus is an active volcano located on Ross Island in Antarctica.
  • Barren Island is an island located in the Andaman Sea, dominated by Barren Volcano, the only confirmed active volcano in South Asia.
  • Mount Fuji located on Honshu Island in an active volcano in Japan. Presently Mount Vesuvius (Italy) is an a active volcano. Mount St. Helens is a volcano located in Skamania County, Washington, in the Pacific Northwest region of the United States. It is also known as the 'Fujiyama of America'.

(2) Dormant Volcanoes- A dormant volcano is one that has not erupted recently but is expected to do so again. Kilimanjaro volcano of Tanzania. It has three main volcanic cones- Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira. Among these peaks Kibo is dormant while Mawenzi and Shira are extinct. Damavand of Iran.

(3) Extinct Volcano – Extinct volcanoes are those that scientist consider unlikely to erupt again because the volcano no longer has a magma supply. For example- Kulal (Kenya) in Africa and Koh-e-Sultan of Pakistan.

Chapter 113

The Earthquake

15 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (15 points)
  • An earthquake is the shaking of the surface of the Earth, resulting from the sudden release of energy in the earth’s lithosphere that creates seismic waves. An earthquake's point of initial rupture is called its seismic focus or hypocenter. The epicenter is the point at ground level directly above the hypocenter. The epicenter is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the hypocenter. All natural earthquakes occur in the lithosphere. There are three basic types of seismic waves –

(1) Primary Waves (P-wave) – They are similar to sound waves. They are also known as longitudinal waves. P-waves travel faster than any other waves. Their intensity of travel depends upon the density of the rock they encounter. Since they are the fastest traveling seismic wave, they are the first signal from an earthquake to arrive at any affected location or at a seismograph. P–waves may be transmitted through gases, liquids and solids.

(2) Secondary Waves (S-waves) – They are similar to light waves. They are also known as transverse waves. These waves arrive after the primary waves and travel slower than the P-waves. The S-waves can travel only through solid materials.

(3) Surface Waves (L-waves) – These waves travel slower than the other two waves and can travel only through the surface of the earth. Surface waves travel around the globe before reaching the epicenter. Surface waves are the most damaging of all the waves. Surface waves are of two types

(i) Love waves (ii) Rayleigh waves. In these two waves Love waves have higher speed.

  • The magnitude of an earthquake is the indication of the energy released.
  • The magnitude of the earthquake is measured on the Richter scale and intensity on Mercalli scale. The Richter scale was invented in the year 1935 by Charles Francis Richter. The Richter scale is a logarithmic scale whose base is 10. Each step represents a ten-fold increase in amplitude on the seismogram, whereas in terms of energy, each whole number increase corresponds to an increase of about 32 times (31.6) the amount of energy released. Every point on the scale (earthquake waves) denotes an energy release, equivalent to 6 ounces of TNT (Trinitrotoluene).
  • Seismometer is used to measure earthquake waves. The term tsunami is borrowed from the Japanese meaning harbor wave.
  • Tsu means Harbor and nami means waves. Tsunami is caused by earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and other underwater explosions and their destructive power can be enormous affecting entire ocean basins.
  • The Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear disaster was an nuclear accident at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant initiated primarily by a tsunami following an earthquake on 11 March 2011. It led to a nuclear meltdown and the release of radioactivity in the area.
  • The Ring of Fire is a major area in the basin of the Pacific Ocean where many earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur. The Ring of Fire is sometimes called Circum Pacific belt. About 90% of the world’s earthquakes occur along the Ring of Fire.
  • There are four main conditions for the occurrence of earthquakes in this region – (1) Point of interaction between sea and land (2) Young fold mountainous region (3) Volcanic Activity (4) Plate tectonics – movement and collision of plates.
  • The region consists of Chile, California, Alaska, Japan, Philippines, New Zealand etc.
  • The Northwestern part of the India subcontinent is an earthquake prone area. This is because it is the convergence zone of Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates.
  • The earthquake-prone regions of India are included in the Mid-Continental Belt. The Belt starts from Cape Verde and includes Atlantic Ocean, Mediterranean Sea, and young fold mountain ranges like the Alps, Caucasus and Himalayas. The Mid-Atlantic Belt is a mid ocean belt.

Plate tectonics → developed in the late 1960s by many (Wilson, Morgan, Parker, McKenzie, Harry Hess), so 'given by H.H. Hess in 1967' is false; it rests on sea-floor spreading.

Key facts from the book (40 points)
  • A mountain range is a series of mountains arranged in a linear manner and connected by high ground.
  • Mountains have a steep slope and pointed summits. Though plateaus are also elevated structures. The main difference between a plateau and a mountain is that the mountain is an elevated, pointed structure whereas a plateau is an elevated area with a flat top.
  • Most geologists classify a mountain as a landform that rises at least 1000 metres or more above its surrounding areas, landforms having elevation less than 1000 metres are generally classified as hills. Thus those areas having an elevation of 1000 m above sea level and also a high relative height in that area are considered to be mountainous regions. Mountains occupy approx. 25% of the Earth's land area however supports only 12% of the global population.
  • British Columbia is called a Sea of Mountains, a name given by Molyneux St. John, in his book “The Sea of Mountains: An account of Lord Dufferin’s Tour Through British Columbia in 1876."
  • Fold mountains – are mountains that are formed mainly by the effect of folding of layers within the upper part of the Earth’s crust.
  • The Andes is the most important mountain range in South America and also the largest mountain range in the world. It has a length of 7000 km. to 8900 km according to different standard sources. The highest peak of Andes is Aconcagua (6962 m).
  • The Rocky Mountain range is the most important mountain range of North America with an approximate length of 4800 km. The highest peak of the Rockies is Mount Elbert (4401 m). The Himalayas of South Asia are located at the northern most point of India. Their approximate length is 2500 km. The highest mountain peak in the world i.e., Mount Everest also known as Sagarmatha or Chomolungma (8848.86 m), along with the other highest peaks, is situated in the Himalaya Mountain Range.
  • The Southern Alps are situated in the western part of the South Island of New Zealand. Their tallest peak is Aoraki/ Mount Cook.
  • The Alps are the highest and most extensive mountain range system that is entirely in Europe.
  • Its highest peak is Mont Blanc (4807 mt). The Alps are the most prominent example of young fold Mountains.
  • The Atlas mountain Range of Africa stretches around 2500 km through Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia.
  • Block mountains – Block mountains are formed as a result of faulting caused by tensile and compressive forces. They are also known as fault block mountains or horst mountains. Block mountains represent the upstanding part of the ground between two faults or on either side of a rift valley.
  • The Sierra Nevada mountain of California (USA) is the world’s most extensive block mountains range.
  • The Black Forest of Germany and Vosges of France are some more examples of block mountains.
  • Salt Range of Pakistan is also an example of block mountains.
  • Dome Mountain - The interior of the earth is hot enough to melt rocks. Melted rock sequences together into vast pools of magma beneath the ground. Since it’s less dense than the surrounding rock, it makes its way upward to the surface. If the magma reaches the surface you get a volcano, but if the magma pushes up but doesn’t actually crack through the surface, you get a dome mountain.
  • The Cincinnati Arch of USA, Black Hills, Bighorns are some examples of dome mountains. Fujiyama of Japan and Cotopaxi of Ecuador are also examples of domed mountains.
  • Mixed Mountains – When a lot of complexity is found in the formation of any mountain range then the mountain is called a mix mountain or a complex mountain. For example, Sierra Nevada and Anaconda Mountains Range of the USA.

(v) Residual Mountains – Residual Mountains are formed as a result of erosion of an existing elevated area. They are also called mountains of denudation. For example - Pennines (Europe), Appalachian (North America), Aravallis (India) etc.

  • White Mountains are situated in New Hampshire and Maine (USA)..
  • Black Mountains is situated in the State of North Carolina, USA. It is a part of the Great Appalachian Range.

  • The tallest peak of this range is Corno Grande (2,914 m).
  • The Dinaric Alps are a mountain range in Europe. They stretch from Italy through Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and Kosovo to Albania.
  • The Jura Mountains extend in the countries, France and Switzerland.
  • The Pyrenees are a range of mountains in southwest Europe that forms a natural border between Spain and France. It also separates the Iberian Peninsula from the rest of continental Europe and extends for about 491 km from the Bay of Biscay to the Mediterranean Sea.
  • The Great Dividing Range or the Eastern Highlands is Australia’s most substantial mountain range and the third longest land- based range in the world. Its highest point is Mount Kosciuszko located in New South Wales Australia. The elevation of Mount Kosciuszko is 2,228 m.
  • Denali is also known as Mount McKinely is the highest mountain peak in North America with a summit elevation of 6,190 m above sea level. On August 2015, it was decided to change the name of Denali.
  • Mount Elbrus is an extinct volcano in the Caucasus Mountains and is considered the highest (5642 m) mountain in Europe and Russia.
  • Mount Kilimanjaro is a dormant volcano in Tanzania. It is the highest mountain in Africa (5895 m above sea level).
  • The Allegheny Mountain Range is a part of the Appalachian Mountain Range of North America.
  • The Cantabrian Mountain Range is a system of a mountain range in Spain. Mount Mackenzie is located in Canada.
  • The Golan Heights is located in the Middle East. It is a basaltic plateau located in the southwest of Syria. Since the 1967 six-day war, the western 2/3rd of the Golan heights has been occupied and administered by Israel and by 1981 it was totally annexed by Israel.
  • Alps, Andes and Himalayas belong to the Tertiary Period. Apart from them Rockies and Atlas Mountain Ranges also belong to Tertiary Period.
  • The Appalachians belong to Caledonian Era.
  • The Aravalli range of India belongs to the Pre-Cambrian Era.
  • Black Forest, Vosges, Tien Shan, Nan Shan, Gobi, etc. are examples of Hercynian Orogeny.

Chapter 116

The Plateaus

7 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (17 points)
  • A plateau, also called a high plain or a tableland, is an area of land with relatively flat terrain that rises significantly above the surrounding region and often has one or more steep sides.
  • Plateaus can be formed by a number of processes

Glacial Plateau- Plateaus formed by the erosional and depositional processes of glaciers on mountain ranges, making their tops flat and sitting between other mountain ranges.

  • Fluvial Plateau- These plateaus have been formed by continuous deposits of fluvial sediments brought by the rivers. The Panna Plateau, Bhander Plateau, Rewa Plateau and Rohtas Plateau are some examples of Fluvial Plateaus. Intermontane Plateau- These are high plateaus enclosed by mountain ranges and are among the most widely distributed and topographically diverse plateau types. Intermontane plateaus are landforms that are surrounded by mountain rims, these plateaus are enclosed by high mountain chains; they are the highest plateaus in the world.
  • The Tibetan Plateau is also known as Qinghai-Tibetan covers an area of approximately 2.5 million sq. km and has an average elevation of4500 m. Chang Tang is located in the western and northern Tibet extending into the southern edges of Xinjiang as well as southeastern Ladakh (India). It is the highest plateau in the world and a good example of an intermontane plateau.
  • The Pamir Knot is known as the Roofofthe World. Note: - The term roof of the world is first used for Pamir Knot, however it is now also used to refer to the Tibetan Plateau.
  • The southern border of Central Asia is determined by the Pamir Knot.
  • The Pamir Plateau in Central Asia is at the junction of the Himalayas with Tien Shan, Karakoram, Kunlun, Hindu Kush and Suleman ranges. They are among the world’s highest mountains. The Bolivia, Peru and Colombia Plateaus of South America and the Mexican Platea of Mexico are also some examples of Intermontane Plateaus. Piedmont Plateau-The name Piedmont comes from the French term for the same physical region, literally meaning ‘foothill’, ultimately from Latin “Pedemontium” meaning at the foothills of mountains.
  • The Piedmont Plateau region located in the Eastern United States and the Patagonia Plateaus of South America are great examples of Piedmont Plateaus. The Patagonia Plateau of South America is very rich in mineral resources.

Domed Plateaus- These are formed when a landmass is uplifted by folding into a broad dome. The Plateau of Ozark (USA) is a good example of a domed Plateau.

  • Continental Plateau- A Continental Plateau is a broad protuberance of the surface of the lithosphere coinciding approximately with a continent but including also the continental shelf. The Indian Peninsula, the Arabian Plateau, Plateau of Australia and the South African Plateau etc. are examples of Continental Plateaus.
  • The Iberian Peninsula also known as Iberia is located in the southwest corner of Europe. The peninsula is principally divided between Spain and Portugal, comprising most of their territory. It is the second largest European peninsula, after the Scandinavian Peninsula. The Meseta plateau of the Iberian Peninsula is located in Spain and has an average elevation of 610-760 m. The capital of Spain Madrid is located at its center.

Coastal Plateau- A plateau located near sea coasts is classified as a Coastal Plateau. India’s Coromandel Coast is an example of a Coastal plain.

Volcanic Plateau- A volcanic plateau is a plateau produced by volcanic activity. Chiefly there are two types:

(a) Lava Plateaus- formed by highly fluid basaltic lava during numerous successive eruptions through numerous vents without violent explosions.

(b) Pyroclastic Plateau- Plateaus are produced by massive pyroclastic flow and they are underlain by pyroclastic rocks: agglomerates, tephra, volcanic ashes cemented into tuffs, the magic offelsics composition. Pyroclastic Plateaus are also called ignimbrite plateaus.

  • Plateaus of New Zealand, South Africa, North and South Argentina, Brazil, Western USA, Mexico, France and Siberia are some examples of a Volcanic Plateaus. The Plateau of Peninsular India is also an example of a Volcanic Plateau.

Tibetan (Qinghai-Tibetan) Plateau → average elevation over 4500 m (nearest option 5 km); area about 2.5 million sq km. Must know

The Valley

12 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (17 points)
  • A valley is a low area between hills or mountains typically with a river flowing through it. In geology a valley is a long depression with very little width.
  • A rift valley is a lowland region formed by the interaction of Earth tectonic plates. It is a linear-shaped lowland between several highlands and mountain ranges created by the action of a geological rift or fault.
  • A rift valley is formed on a divergent plate boundary, a crustal extension or spreading apart of the surface, which is subsequently further dependent on the forces of erosion.
  • The Death Valley situated mainly in California (USA) is an example of a rift valley.
  • Devils Golf Course is a large salt pan on the floor of Death Valley, located in the northern Mojave Desert within Death Valley National Park. The park is located mainly in eastern California.
  • In the Holocene era this area was covered with water reaching a depth of 30 ft. When the water of the region dried up it left behind the dissolved salt in it.
  • Death Valley is the point of the lowest elevation in North America (-86 m) and the second lowest point in the Western Hemisphere only after Laguna del Carbon of Argentina (-105 m). During summers the temperature in Death Valley can rise up to 56.7°C. It is the hottest and driest place in the USA. Recently it was declared the hottest place on the planet (from the point of view of air temperature).
  • The Panjshir Valley (literally the valley of five lions) is a valley in northeastern Afghanistan, north of Kabul, near the Hindu Kush Mountain Range. It is divided by the Panjshir River. The valley was a major battleground during the Soviet war.
  • The Taylor Valley of Antarctica was discovered by Robert Falcon Scott in the year 1903. He designated this valley as the Valley of the Dead.

Spreading across about 1.7 million sq.km, it is located between the Great Dividing Range and the medial uplands.

Chapter 118

The Arid Regions/ Deserts

25 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (22 points)
  • Desert is a barren area of landscape where little precipitation occurs and consequently, living conditions are hostile for plants and animals. About 1/3rd of the land surface of the world is arid or semiarid. Regions receiving precipitation of less than 25 cm annually are categorized as deserts. Deserts can be classified by the amount of precipitation, by the temperature that prevails, by the causes of their dryness or by their geographical location.
  • Tropical hot deserts are generally found on the continental interiors and often western side between 15° to 30° north or south of the equator. Most of the major deserts of the world lie in areas crossed by the trade winds.
  • According to German scientist Dr. Gerhard Knies, the amount of energy that is received from the sun by the word's desearts in 6 hours is more than the amount of energy consumed by the entire humankind in a year. Hence deserts are a very prominent source of renewable energy.
  • The Sahara Desert is the largest non-polar desert in the world. The desert comprises much of North Africa, excluding the fertile regions on the Mediterranean Sea coast. It occupies a total area of 3600000 sq. miles. The Sahara covers large parts of Algeria, Chad, Egypt, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Morocco, Niger, Western Sahara, Sudan and Tunisia. The main phenomena behind the formation of African and Euro Asian deserts are –

1. Their proximity to cold ocean currents which run along the west coast. These cold ocean currents cool the air and make it harder for the air to hold moisture.

2. Most of these deserts are located far away from the moisture-laden trade winds.

  • The Atacama is a desert plateau in South America on the Pacific Coast, west of Andes Mountains. It is the driest desert in the world.
  • The Atacama Desert is rich in metallic mineral resources such as copper, gold, silver and iron, as well as non-metallic minerals including important deposits ofboron, lithium, sodium nitrate and potassium salts. It is the world’s largest supplier of sodium nitrate. The Atacama Desert occupies the narrow coast of northern Chile and southern Peru.
  • The Kalahari Desert is located in the Southern Hemisphere. The Kalahari Desert is a large semi-arid sandy savanna in Southern Africa, extending for 9,30,000 square kilometers covering much of Botswana, parts of Namibia and regions of South Africa.
  • The Dasht-e-Lut is a large salt desert located in the provinces of Kerman and Sistan and Baluchistan, Iran. According to NASA, it is the world’s hottest desert. The Aqua satellite of NASA, in the year 2005 measured the surface temperature of this desert and found it to be as high as 70.7°C, making it the hottest desert (based on surface temperature) in the world.
  • The Thar Desert, also known as the Great Indian Desert is a large arid region in the northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent and forms a natural boundary between India and Pakistan. It is the largest desert in South Asia. The Thar Desert is the most densely populated desert in the world, with a population density of 83 people per/km².
  • The Taklamakan Desert is a desert in southwestern Xinjiang Province in north west China. It is bounded by the Kunlun mountains to the south, the Pamir mountains to the west Tian Shan to the north, and the Gobi Desert in the east.
  • The Sonoran Desert occurs primarily in Mexico. More than two thirds of its total area is in Baja California, Baja California Sur, and the state of Sonora. It covers large parts of the southwestern United States in Arizona and California. The western portion of the United States – Mexico border passes through the Sonoran Desert.
  • The Karakum Desert, is a desert in Central Asia. Its name means "black sand" in Turkic languages, in reference to the dark soil that lies beneath the sandy surface of much of the desert. It occupies much of the area of Turkmenistan and a smaller part of Kazakhstan.
  • The Karakum Desert is home to the Darvaza gas Crater. The area has significant oil and natural gas deposits.
  • The Gibson Desert is a large desert that covers a large dry area in the State of Western Australia. It is the 5th largest desert in Australia, after the Great Victoria Deseart, Great Sandy Deseart, Tanami Deseart and Simpson Desert.
  • Al Nafud is a desert in Northern Saudi Arabia. The discovery of approximately 88000-90000 years old fossilized human finger bone in Al Nafud in 2016 by Dr. Mathieu Duval of Griffith University provided the earliest evidence of modern humans outside Africa and the Levant.
  • The Rub’al Khali Desert is located in Saudi Arabia, Oman, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen are the largest contiguous sand desert in the world.Famous oil fields, Shaybah and Ghawar are located in this desert.
  • The Kyzylkum Desert is divided between Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. The desert is well known for its deposits of gold, uranium, copper, aluminium and silver, natural gas and oil.
  • Dasht-e-Kavir is a large desert located in Iran.
  • The Gobi Desert is a cold desert found in a temperate region. It covers parts of northern China and of southern Mongolia. The Gobi Desert is notable in history as part of the great Mongol Empire and as the location of several important cities along the Silk Road.
  • Patagonia Desert is a cold desert and also the largest desert in Argentina. It is located primarily in Argentina with small parts in Chile and is bounded by the Andes, to its west and the Atlantic Ocean to its east.

Chapter 119

The Grasslands

15 facts · 3 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (7 points)
  • A grassland is an area of land that mostly contains grasses. There are wild grasses and there may be some trees. From the hot equatorial region to the cold polar region, grasslands are found all over the world. However, their characteristics and physical attributes change with the change in the climate. Thus, based on the climatic factors the grassland can be categorized into two parts

1. Tropical Grasslands- These are located near the equator (10° to 25° North or South Latitudes), between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn. The Tropical Grasslands are also known as Savannas. The Savanna grasslands are mostly found in East Africa. They are also found in the Orinoco basin (Venezuela and Colombia), Brazil, Honduras and the southern parts of India. These grasslands are known by different names in different parts of the world. In Africa, they are known as Savanna, Llanos in Venezuela and Colombia. Campos in Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina and Uruguay. Selvas (Selva) are tropical evergreen rainforests in the Amazon Basin.

  • 2. Temperate Grasslands- Located between 30° to 60° North and South Latitudes. Due to greater territorial expansion in the Northern Hemisphere, these grasslands (in Northern Hemisphere) may extend up 60° North Latitude. The major temperate grasslands include the Velds of Africa, the Pampas of Argentina, the Steppes of Eurasia, the Prairies of North America, and the Downs of Australia.
  • The Prairie grasslands are found in North America.
  • The Pampas grasslands are mostly found in Argentina, though they also extend to Uruguay and Brazil.
  • The temperate grasslands found in Eurasia (Eastern Europe and Central Asia) are known as steppes. The temperate grasslands found in South Africa are called velds.
  • Downs are temperate grasslands found in Australia.

Steppes → Russia; Prairies → U.S.A.; Velds (Welds) → South Africa; Downs → Australia. Tropical grasslands: Savanna (Africa), Llanos (Venezuela, Colombia), Campos (Brazil).

Chapter 121

Dependent Territories

7 facts · 0 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (35 points)
  • A dependent territory is a territory that does not possess full political independence or sovereignty as a sovereign state yet remains politically outside the controlling state's integral area. Dependent Territories under France:

Martinique, French Polynesia, French Guiana, Reunion, New Caledonia, etc.

Dependent Territories Under Denmark:

  • Greenland is an autonomous region of the Kingdom of Denmark. However, from a geographical point of view, Greenland is a part of the North American continent. Three-quarters of Greenland (about 80%) is covered by permanent ice sheets.
  • The Faroe Islands are a North Atlantic archipelago, located north of the United Kingdom and about halfway between Norway and Iceland. It is an autonomous region of the Kingdom of Denmark.

Dependent Territories under the United States of America:-

  • American Samoa is an unincorporated territory of the United States located in the South Pacific Ocean east of Australia. Since 1900 CE the islands have been an unincorporated territory of the United States of America.
  • Puerto Rico is an unincorporated territory of the USA located in the northeast Caribbean Sea, southeast of Miami, Florida. Puerto Rico was discovered by Christopher Columbus in 1493 CE.
  • The U.S. Virgin Islands in the Caribbean is an unincorporated and organized territory of the United States. It is located east of Puerto Rico.
  • Midway Atoll is an unorganized, unincorporated territory of the United States. It is located in the North Pacific Ocean. Dependent Territories under Portugal:
  • The Azores are an autonomous region of Portugal. It is an archipelago composed of nine volcanic islands in the North Atlantic Ocean.
  • Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal. It is a volcanic archipelago situated in the North Atlantic Ocean.

Dependent Territories of Spain:

  • The Canary Islands are a Spanish archipelago and the southernmost autonomous community of Spain located in the Atlantic Ocean.
  • Ceuta is a Spanish autonomous region on the North Coast of Africa, separated from Cadiz province on the Spanish mainland by the Strait of Gibraltar.
  • Melilla is a Spanish autonomous city located on the north coast of Africa, sharing a border with Morocco.
  • The Balearic Islands are an archipelago of Spain in the western Mediterranean Sea, near the eastern coast of the Iberian Peninsula.

Dependent Territories under Norway:

  • Bouvet Island is an island in the southern part of the Atlantic Ocean. It belongs to Norway and is not subject to the Antarctic Treaty (which says that land south of 60° S, including Antarctica, does not belong to any country). Apart from it Peter I Island (Antarctica) and Queen Maud Land (Antarctica) are also dependent territories under Norway. Dependent Territories under the United Kingdom:-
  • The Pitcairn Island are a group of islands in the southern Pacific Ocean. They are governed by the United Kingdom.
  • Saint Helena is an island of volcanic origin in the South Atlantic Ocean. It is named after Saint Helena of Constantinople. It is part of the British Overseas Territory.
  • Gibraltar is an overseas territory of the United Kingdom. It is in southwest Europe on the Mediterranean Sea. It is situated at the southernmost point of the Iberian Peninsula.
  • The Turks and Caicos Islands are also under the jurisdiction of Great Britain. They are located in the Caribbean Sea, near the Bahamas.
  • Falkland Islands are a group of islands in South America (in the Atlantic Ocean). They are an overseas territory of the United Kingdom.
  • British Indian Ocean Territory is a dependency of the United Kingdom. It is located to the northeast of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. The region includes many small islands in the Indian Ocean, but the two most important, are the atolls of the Chaos Archipelago and the largest island of the region Diego Garcia (UK/US joint military base is located here). The claim to the region has been suspended since the Antarctic Treaty came into force in 1961. Dependent Territories under New Zealand:
  • The Cook Islands are a group of islands in the Southern Pacific. Its capital is Avarua.
  • Niue is an island country in the South Pacific situated east of Tonga. It is commonly known as the “Rock of Polynesia”. It has its own government but it is an associated state of New Zealand.
  • Tokelau is a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean the territory belongs to New Zealand.
  • The Ross Dependency is an area of Antarctica claimed by New Zealand. The dependency takes its name from Sir James Clark Ross, who discovered the Ross Sea.

Dependent Territories under Australia:

  • Christmas Island is an island belonging to Australia. It is in the Indian Ocean, 2605 km northwest of Perth in Western Australia and 500 km south of Jakarta, Indonesia.
  • Cocos Islands are a territory of Australia.
  • Norfolk Island is a small volcanic island and is a territory of Australia.

Dependent Territories under Russia:

  • Chechnya is a Republic of Russia and is part of the North Caucasus Federal District. Politically it has the status of a Republic. The state was established on 10 December, 1992. The capital of Chechnya is Grozny.

Chapter 124

International Border Lines

10 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (13 points)
  • It is very important to know about the international boundary lines between major countries.
  • The Rio Grande is one of the principal rivers in the United States and Mexico. It forms part of United States Mexico border.
  • Lake Victoria of Africa also known as Lake Victoria Nyanza is the second largest freshwater lake in the world by surface are. The Lake’s are shared by three countries Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. The lake thus creates an international border between Uganda-Tanzania, Uganda Kenya and Kenya-Tanzania.
  • The McMahon Line is the effective boundary between India and China. India claims the McMahon Line to be a permanent line of the settlement of borders whereas China claims it to be temporary in nature. China does not even recognize the Shimla Treaty.
  • The Maginot Line constructed after the 1st World War is named after the French Minister of War Andre Maginot. The line was built near France's eastern border with Germany and the annexed countries.
  • The Alpine Line or Little Maginot Line separates the borders of France and Italy.
  • Radcliffe Line is the boundary demarcation line between India Pakistan and India-Bangladesh.
  • The 49th parallel (49°N Latitude) north forms the United States–Canada border.
  • The 38th parallel (38°N latitude) north forms the border between North and South Korea.
  • The Oder-Neisse Line is the basis of the international border between Germany and Poland.
  • The Durand Line is the international border between Pakistan and Afghanistan and between India and Afghanistan.
  • The Hindenburg Line was a German defensive position built during the winter of 1916-17 on the Western Front during the First World War. It forms the border between Germany, Belgium and France.
  • The Mannerheim Line forms the borderline between Poland and Russia.

Chapter 127

Geographical Sobriquets

20 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (21 points)
  • There are many countries in this world that are often known by their geographical sobriquets.
  • Midnight Sun is a natural phenomenon that occurs in the summer months in places north of the Arctic Circle or south of the Antarctic Circle when the sun remains visible at local midnight.
  • Around the summer solstice (approximately 21 June in the Northern Hemisphere and 22 December in the Southern Hemisphere), the sun is visible for a full 24 hours. Thus countries like Norway which lies in the Arctic region experience 24 hours of daylight, a reason why it is often called the Land of Midnight sun. Norway is the best-suited example of the phenomenon of Midnight Sun even though parts of other countries like Canada, Sweden, Russia, Iceland, and Finland are also located north of the Arctic Circle and experience a Midnight Sun.
  • In the Southern Hemisphere there is no country situated between the Antarctic Circle and the South Pole.
  • Out of the 11131 species of birds found on this planet, around 3698 bird species are found in South America. Hence South America is also known as the 'Bird Continent'.
  • 'Mistress of the Eastern Sea' is a geographical Sobriquet of Sri Lanka. Sri Lanka is located north of the equator. The country lies to the South-East of the Indian sub-continent separated by Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait. Sri Lanka is located in the Indian Ocean and is often referred to as the 'The Pearl of Indian Ocean'. Singapore is called the 'Gateway to Asia'.
  • Thailand is the country that is also called the 'Land of white elephants', as it has a large number of White elephants and the white elephants are the symbol of royal power in Thailand. It is believed that if the King of Thailand was unsatisfied with the work of any of his associates, he would gift him a white elephant, which would turn the man bankrupt.
  • Nippon refers to Japan. It means the 'Land of Rising Sun'.
  • Thus Japan is known as the Land of the Rising Sun.
  • The thousands of lakes in Finland are the reason why the country’s nickname is 'The Land of a Thousand Lakes'.
  • South Korea is known as the 'Land of The Morning Calm'. Istanbul, the former capital of Turkiye is a major tourist destination. Since it is a transcontinental city it is also known as the 'Gateway of the West'.
  • Venice is known as the 'City of Canals'. Venice is one of the most beautiful cities in the world. Venice (Italy) is also known as 'City of Dreams'.
  • Osaka is a designated city in the Kansai region of Japan. It is also known as 'Manchester of the East'. However historically the city of Osaka is also known as 'Nation’s Kitchen'.
  • The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge that connects the two ends of the Bay of San Francisco. It is the reason why San Francisco is also known as the 'City of Golden Gate'.
  • The problem of smoking became so severe in Chicago that an ordinance had to be passed in 2005 to ban smoking. Chicago is hence also known as City of Smokers. The Eiffel Tower is a wrought – iron lattice tower in Paris, France. It is named after the engineer Gustave Eiffel, whose company designed and built the tower; including the 24 meter long antenna. The tower is 1083 feet (330 m.) tall.
  • Pamir Knot is known as the roofofthe world. The Pamir Knot makes up the Southern border of Central Asia.
  • Bahrain is known as the Island of Pearls. It is also known as 'Pearl of Persian Gulf'.
  • Lake Baikal is located in Siberia (Russia). It is also known as 'Pearl of Siberia.'
  • Buenos Aires is the capital of Argentina and is also known as 'Paris of South America'.

Chapter 128

The Hydrosphere

14 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (24 points)
  • The Hydrosphere is the total volume of water on the surface of our planet. Although the Earth’s Hydrosphere has been around for longer than 4 billion years, it continues to change and rise. This is caused by seafloor spreading and continental drift. Hydrosphere occupies more than 2/3 of the total surface of the Earth.
  • Hydrosphere covers about 71% (70.9%) of Earth’s surface. There is only one world ocean but the continents divide the ocean into five largest distinct parts -
(i)Pacific Ocean (155557000 sq. km)
(ii)Atlantic Ocean (76762000 sq. km)
(iii)Indian Ocean (68556000 sq. km)
(iv)Southern Ocean (20327000 sq. km)
(v)Arctic Ocean (14056000 sq. km)

The Pacific Ocean is the largest in the world.

  • Oceanic Relief is a part of lithospheric Relief.
  • Hypsographic curve describes the distribution of Earth's surface elevations and ocean depth relative to sea level. We read the hypsographic curve like a graph with an x-axis (horizontal) and a y-axis (vertical). The x-axis tells us the elevation of the province. The curved line on the graph tells us about the provinces - where we see a change in the slope of the line, we are looking at a different province.
  • The oceanic crust differs strikingly from the continental crust with respect to rock types, structure, landforms, age and origin. Four major divisions in the ocean relief are

1. Continental Shelf - It is the submerged margin of continental mass extending from the shore to the first prominent slope.

2. Continental Slope - The slope that extends from the continental shelf down to the ocean deep.

3. Continental Rise - This is the gently sloping seafloor lying at the foot of the continental slope leading gradually into the Abyssal Plain.

4. Abyssal Plain - This is the large expanse of very smooth ocean floor found at depths of 3000 to 6000 meters In fact they are the most widespread landforms on the Earth and occupy almost 76% of the total oceanic area.

  • Oceanic trenches are narrow, deep depressions in the seafloor representing the line of subduction of an oceanic lithosphere plate. The ocean trenches are the lowest areas on Earth’s surface and occupy almost 7% of the ocean’s relief. They have very steep slopes. Examples of oceanic trenches include the Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep in the Marina Trench), Tonga Trench and Kuril-Kamchatka Trench etc. Other important oceanic reliefs are -

(i) Oceanic Ridge - formed by lava, that erupts beneath the sea and cools to form solid rocks.

(ii) Mid Ocean Ridge - an underwater mountain system formed by plate tectonics.

(iii) Guyot - A Guyot, also known as a tablemount is an isolated underwater volcanic mountain with a flat top below the surface of the sea. They are commonly found in the Pacific Ocean, but they have been identified in all the oceans except the Arctic Ocean.

(iv) Submarine Canyon - Narrow steep-sided valleys that cut into continental slopes and continental rises of the ocean.

(v) Fracture Zone - A linear oceanic feature often hundreds, even thousands of kilometers long. They are a consequence of plate tectonics.

Similarly, other ocean relief features include island arcs, atolls, coral reefs, submerged volcanoes, sea-scarps etc.

  • Mid Atlantic Ridge is a mid-ocean ridge, a divergent tectonic plate or constructive plate boundary located on the floor of the Atlantic Ocean and part of the most extensive mountain range in the world. In the North Atlantic it separates the Eurasian and North American plates and in South Atlantic it separates the African & South American plates.
  • The Ninety East Ridge is a ridge on the Indian Ocean floor named for its near by parallel strike along the 90th meridian at the center of the Eastern Hemisphere.
  • Examples of such islands in the Indian Ocean are - Lakshadweep, Maldives, Chagos, Amsterdam Island, Saint Paul, Kerguelen Islands etc.
  • Datum line is the horizontal line to sea level used to measure heights and depths.
  • 96.5% of the total water present in the ocean is saline in nature. Out of the remaining 2.5% is fresh water. 1.7% are in the form of glaciers and polar ice. Hence, less than 1% of fresh water resources is available for use.
  • Out of the total available fresh water, 68.7% is inaccessible as it is in the form of glaciers and ice caps. 30.1% is in the form of groundwater, 0.3% is in the form of surface water and only 0.9% is in the form of other freshwater sources.

OMT is measured to the 26°C isotherm, at 59 m (not 129 m) in SW Indian Ocean in Jan-Mar; Jan-Mar OMT helps predict monsoon rainfall vs long-term mean.

Chapter 129

Important Seas of the World

21 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (16 points)

In terms of geography, a sea is a part of the ocean partially enclosed by land. Seas are smaller than the oceans and are usually located where the land and ocean meet.

Some important seas of the world are as follows-

  • The South China Sea is a marginal sea that is a part of the Pacific Ocean. It is located between China, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei, Indonesia and Vietnam. Its maximum depth is about 5560 m.
  • The Bering Sea is also a marginal sea of the Pacific Ocean. Covering a total area of 2520000 sq. km, it has a maximum depth of 3500 m.
  • The Mediterranean Sea is a sea connected to the Atlantic Ocean. It is the largest of all seas enclosed by land. It extends between North Africa, Southern Europe, Anatolia and Levant. The maximum known depth of the Mediterranean Sea is 5267 m.
  • The Black Sea is a marginal sea of the Atlantic Ocean, located in the south-east of Europe. The Black Sea is surrounded by Europe, Caucasus and the Anatolia Peninsula.
  • The Caspian sea is the world’s largest inland body of water, and world’s largest saltwater lake. It is also the world’s largest lake. It covers a total area of 371000 sq. km. It has borders with Russia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Kazakhstan.
  • The Sea of Azov is a sea in Eastern Europe, that is almost completely enclosed by land, having just a narrow opening into the Black Sea via Strait of Kerch. The sea borders Ukraine in the North, Russia in the east and Crimea Peninsula in the west.
  • The Aral Sea is an important water body in Central Asia. It lies between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.
  • Sargasso Sea is a water body in the North Atlantic Ocean. The sea is bounded by Gulf Stream on the west boundary, North Atlantic Current/Drift on the North, Canary Current in the East, Azores Current on the northeast, Antilles Current on the South-West and North Atlantic Equatorial Current on the south. The sea is named after the Sargasso seaweed, which is found in abundance in the region.
  • The Tyrrhenian Sea is a part of the Mediterranean Sea off the western coast of Italy. The sea is bounded by Corsica, Sardinia, Italy and Sicily. The Tyrrhenian Sea is linked to other seas of the region through the Strait of Messina, Strait of Bonifacio and Corsica Channel.
  • The countries of Africa surrounding the Mediterranean Sea are Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco.
  • The Middle-Eastern Asian country of Jordan does not have any boundaries with the Mediterranean Sea.
  • Turkiye is a transcontinental country located mainly in western Asia with a small portion of it lying in south-east Europe. Turkiye is bordered by the Black Sea in the North, Mediterranean Sea in South Aegean Sea in West and the Sea of Marmara in the Northwest.
  • The Black Sea lies to the north and the Mediterranean Sea lies to the south of Turkiye.
  • Turkiye shares borders with 8 countries which are as follows Bulgaria in the Northwest, Greece in the West, Georgia in the Northeast. Iran and Azerbaijan in the East, Iraq and Syria in the Southeast.

Baku, capital of Azerbaijan → on the Caspian Sea coast; the Caspian is the largest saltwater lake.

Chapter 130

The Ocean Currents

18 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (38 points)
  • An ocean current is a continuous directed movement of sea -water. Surface ocean currents are mainly driven by the prevailing winds and by the rotation of the Earth. Deep-ocean currents, which flow thousands of meters below the ocean surface are driven by differences in water density caused by variation in temperature and salinity. In general, the main cause of ocean currents are wind, differences in water density and tides.

The main causes of ocean currents are–

(i) Differential heating of the equatorial and polar oceans.

(ii) Trade and anti-trade winds

(iii) Coriolis effect

(iv) Variation in salinity and temperature of the oceans.

(v) Configuration of the coastline and ocean floor.

(vi) Gravity

  • The oceanic currents play a huge role in regulating the planet’s temperature.
  • Based on the temperature, the ocean currents can be categorized into two types - warm ocean currents and cold ocean currents.

Factors Responsible for Change in Direction of Ocean Currents Incluid:

(i) Configuration of the coast - When a landmass lies perpendicular to the prevailing current, the obstruction thus caused deviates the current to move parallel to the landmass.

(ii) Ocean floor reliefs - The diversified ocean floor with distinctive reliefs can also affect the oceanic currents and their direction.

(iii) Seasonal Variations - for example, the monsoonal winds change the direction of the ocean currents.

(iv) The Earth’s Rotation - The Earth’s rotation deflects freely moving objects including ocean currents, to the right. In the northern hemisphere, this is a clockwise direction (e.g. the circulation of the Gulf Stream Drift and the Canary Current). In the southern hemisphere it is an anti-clockwise direction (e.g. the Brazilian Current and the West Wind Drift).

  • 1. Currents of Atlantic Ocean -
  • Under the influence of trade winds the North Equatorial Warm Current flows east to west from African coast in the east to the West Indies.
  • Antilles Current - Northeastern coast of South America the North Equatorial Current splits into two branches. One branch flows northward, east of the Antilles (West Indies) as Antilles Current and it joins the Florida Current past the outer Bahamas. The other branch passes into the Caribbean Sea as the Caribbean Current and flows west through the Caribbean Sea, then north through the Yucatan Channel into the Gulf of Maxico.
  • Florida Current - Under the influence of the trade winds the current flows from the GulfofMexico towards the Straits of Florida. Here it adjoins the Antilles Current.
  • Gulf Stream - When the Florida current and Antilles current join together, they are collectively known as the Gulf Stream. The Gulf Stream is a warm and swift Atlantic Ocean current that follows the eastern coastline of the United States.
  • Canary Cold Current - It flows southwestward along the northwest coast of Africa as far south as Senegal before turning westward to join the Atlantic North Equatorial Current.
  • East Greenland Current - The current travels along the eastern coast of Greenland in southward and southwestward.
  • Labrador Cold Current - The current flows from Baffin

Ocean Currents

Bay and the Davis Strait and travels along the coast of Labrador in southward.

  • North Atlantic Drift/Current - The current originates between 45º North Latitude and 45º West Longitude. This current is responsible for carrying the Gulf Stream to Europe. Countries like Norway which are located in a sub-polar region benefit the most from this drift of current. This is because during winters northern Europe receives heavy snowfall, thus the warm North Atlantic Drift/Current prevents extreme cold in the region and also keeps the harbors ice-free. As a result, the North Atlantic Warm Drift/Current is also known as the ‘Blanket of Europe’.

Brazil Current is a warm current. At 40º South Latitude, the Falkland Current meets the Brazil Current. Collectively they flow eastward as South Atlantic Drift. Upon reaching the west coast of Africa the current is diverted northwards as the cold Benguela Current. It brings the cold polar waters of the west drift into tropical latitudes. Driven by the regular southeast trade winds, the Benguela Current moves equatorward in a northwesterly direction to join the South Equatorial Current. This completes the circulation of the currents in the South Atlantic.

2.Currents of Indian Ocean - As in the other oceans, the currents of the South Indian Ocean form a circuit. The South Equatorial Current turns Southward and divides into the Madagascar Current and Mozambique Current. These currents merge as Agulhain Current with the West Wind Drift, flowing eastwards and turning equatorward as the West Australian Current (cool current). In the northern Indian Ocean, there is a complete reversal of the direction of currents between summer and winter, due to the changes in monsoon winds. In summer from June to October, when the dominant wind is the southwest Monsoon, the currents are blown from a south - westerly direction as the southwest Monsoon Drift. This is reversed in winter, beginning in December, when the northeast Monsoon blows the currents from the north-east as the north-east Monsoon Drift.

3. Currents of Pacific Ocean - The pattern of circulation in the Pacific is similar to that of the Atlantic except for modifications that can be expected from the greater size and more open nature of the Pacific.

  • The North Equatorial Current is a current in the Pacific Ocean, originating in the Mid Americas and flowing east to west. The Northeast Trade Winds blow the North Equatorial Current to the coast of the Philippines.
  • Kuroshio Warm Current - After reaching the island of the Philippines the North Equatorial Current flows towards Taiwan and the northwards past Japan. Here, the current is known as Kuroshio Current.
  • California Cold Current - When the North Pacific Drift reaches the western coast of North America it gets bifurcated into two parts. One travels northwards and the other travels southwards along the western coast of North America. The southward-moving current is known as the California current.
  • Alaskan Stream Current - The northward branch of the North Pacific current when it enters the Gulf of Alaska is known as Alaskan warm current. Again it flows along the coast of Alaska, where it is known as the Alaskan stream, which is a cold stream
  • Oyashio Cold Current - The current originates in the Bering Strait and travels in a northsouth direction near the eastern coast of Kamchatka Peninsula.
  • Kurile Current - Passing through the Bering Strait and transporting cold water from the Arctic Sea into the Pacific Ocean and the Sea of Okhotsk. Again passing through the east coast of Sakhalin Island it is joined by the Okhotsk current to meet the warm Japan Current as of the Oyashio.
  • East Australian Warm Current - The East Australian Current sweeps warm water down the east coast of Australia.
  • Peruvian Cold Current - Also known as the Humboldt Current, travels along the west coast of South America.
  • Equatorial Counter Current - Due to North and South Equatorial Currents the Pacific Ocean accumulates a huge amount of water on both sides of the equator. This results in an inbalance in Ocean’s water levels. To current this imbalance equatorial counter currents come into action.

Ocean currents are driven by Earth's rotation, wind and air pressure, and density (temperature, salinity) differences; not by Earth's revolution.

Chapter 131

The salinity of the Ocean

9 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (17 points)

Almost every known chemical element can be found in varying proportions in the ocean.

  • Salinity is the amount of salt dissolved in a body of water. On average, seawater in the world’s oceans has a salinity of approximately 35‰ or 35 parts per thousand. This means that for every 1 kg (1000 grams) of seawater there are 35g of salt dissolved in it.
  • Lands are the main source of salinity in the oceans and rivers are the main carriers. Other factors responsible for ocean salinity are - evaporation, wind, river water, precipitation, ocean currents and volcanoes etc.
  • During an exploration of Challenger Deep in 1884, Dittmar discooured that there are 47 types of salts present in the seas. Out of these 47 types of salts, 7 are the important ones. They are as follows.

  • The maximum contribution to the salinity of the ocean is that of sodium chloride.
  • The salinity of the ocean can be divided into horizontal and vertical parameters. The uncertainty regarding the amount of salinity in the vertical dimension has obstructed the devlopment of a principle for measuring vertical salinity. This is because in some places, salinity increases with depth and vice-versa.
  • The density of ocean water is directly proportional to its salinity. This means that if the density of water increases it is an indicator of an increase in salinity hence with the increase in water density, salinity also increases.
  • The horizontal distribution of salinity in ocean water is expressed as the degree of saltiness of the water, either as a percentage or more often in parts per thousand Variations are shown in salinity distribution maps by isohalines (lines joining places having an equal degree of salinity). Latitudes have a huge impact on the salinity of the oceans. Salinity is lower than the average 34‰ in equatorial waters because of the heavy daily rainfall and high evaporation. Deserts mainly 25º–30º N and S, waters have high salinity because of the high rate of evaporation caused by high temperatures and low humidity. Waters of the polar region have a salinity of less than 35‰ due to the colder climate with little evaporation and because much fresh water is added from the melting of icebergs as well as by several large poleward-bound rivers, e.g. Ob, Lena, Yenisei etc.
  • Maximum salinity is found between 20º-40º North Latitudes where salinity may increase up to 36‰.
  • Ocean water of the Indian Ocean falling between 0º-10º Latitudes has a salinity of 35.14‰ however it decreases to 30‰ in Bay of Bengal. On the contrary the salinity increases upto 36‰ in the Arabian Sea. This is due to a high rate of evaporation and low humidity. Additionally there is much less fresh water carried to the Arabian Sea by west flowing rivers as compared to Bay of Bengal.
  • Among the various seas and Lakes of the world, the Van Lake in Turkiye has a salinity of330‰. The salinity of Dead Sea is 238‰.
  • Salinity in the Northern part of Caspian Sea is 13-14‰, whereas in the southern part of Caspian sea, in the Karabuga Bay, salinity is 300-350‰.
  • The most saline sea is Red Sea with a salinity of 36-41‰.
  • The salinity of the Mediterranean Sea is 37-39‰. In the Caribbean Sea it is 35-36‰ and the salinity of the Persian Gulf is 37-40‰.

Note - World’s lakes with maximum salinity Lake Assal (348‰), Lake Van of Turkiye (330‰), Dead Sea (238‰) and Great Salt Lake (220‰).

  • The world’s most hyper-saline lake is Don Juan Pond in Antarctica, and second to it is Garabogazkol (Turkmenistan), which is a lagoon. It is important to mention here that lake Van of Turkiye is comparatively less saline however the Lake water is strongly alkaline (pH 9.7-9.8).

Halocline → zone where salinity changes rapidly with depth (the salinity gradient).

Chapter 132

High Tide, Low Tide

4 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (10 points)
  • Tides are the rise and fall of sea levels caused by the combined effects of the gravitational forces exerted by the Moon and the Sun, and the rotation of the Earth. The rotation of the Earth creates two forces - the centripetal and centrifugal forces, which play a major role in the formation of tides. This means that the side of the Earth that faces the Moon experiences a gravitational force, greater than that of the Earth itself. Hence we experience high tides. On the other hand the side of Earth that is facing away from moon experiences less gravitational force from the Moon, as a result, we experience high (indirect high tides) tides. Between these two high tides water level goes down this is called low tides (ebb). Thus in the time span of 24 hrs. and 50 minutes (or 52 minutes) we experience two High Tides and two Low Tides.

Moon Moon Syzygy

Sun

Moon

Sun

Moon

  • When the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are aligned in a straight line, we experience a Spring Tide. In astronomy, this situation is known as syzygy. It occurs on a full moon or new moon day. On the other hand, when the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are at a right angle to each other the gravitational forces of these celestial bodies act against each other resulting in Neap Tide. Neap Tide is observed on the 7th or 8th day of each lunar month (14 days appx.) During Neap Tides, there is a decrease of 20% in the Spring Tides whereas the Neap Tides are higher than the normal occurrences.
  • The Moon is the closest celestial body to Earth hence its gravity has a significant impact on our planet. The moon is responsible for the sea waves of the oceans.
  • The effect of Moon on the tidal forces of our planet is 2.17 times greater than that of the Sun.
  • The city of Southampton in England experiences 4 tides every day. This occurs because two tides travel from English Channel and two from the North Sea at different intervals.

Tides → Moon's gravitational pull plus centripetal and centrifugal forces; the indirect high tide (side away from the Moon) → Earth's centrifugal force. Must know

The Oceanic Trenches

6 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (4 points)

Oceanic Trenches are long, narrow trenches that plunge to great depths of5000 fathoms or 30000 feet. Trenches account for approximately 7% of the ocean’s relief Contrary to our expectations, most of the deepest trenches are not located in the midst of the ocean; they are more often found close to the continents, particularly in the Pacific Ocean, where several deep trenches have been found.

  • The Mariana Trench is the deepest trench in the world. It is located in the Pacific Ocean east of Mariana Islands. The Mariana Trench is a crescent- shaped trough. This trench was discovered in 1875 with the help of a survey ship called HMS Challenger. The Mariana Trench was also surveyed in 1951 by the British survey vessel, HMS Challenger II. The estimated depth of the Challenger Deep in Mariana Trench is 11,033 meters. The prominent trenches of the North Pacific Ocean are - Mariana Trench, Kuril Trench, Aleutian Trench and Japan Trench.
  • The prominent trenches of Atlantic Ocean are - Puerto Rico Trench (N. Atlantic Ocean), Romanche Trench (Equatorial Atlantic Ocean) and South- Sandwich Trench (South Atlantic Ocean).
  • The Sunda trench (Old name - Java trench) is the deepest trench in the Indian Ocean. Diamantina Trench is in the Indian Ocean. It is located about 1125 km southwest of the Perth Basin. It is also known as the Diamantina Fracture Zone.

Aleutian Trench → North Pacific; Kermadec → South Pacific; Sunda (Java) → Indian Ocean; South Sandwich → South Atlantic.

Chapter 136

Landforms by River

7 facts · 0 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (6 points)
  • In rivers, erosion, transportation and deposition go on simultaneously from the point of origin to the point where they meet the sea. This process leads to the formation of different terrestrial relief features. Some of them are as follows Gorge - It is a deep narrow section of river valley usually with near vertical rock walls, more generally a narrow valley between hills and mountains. Gorges are formed as a result of continued erosion of mountainous terrain by a river. For Ex: Chisapani Gorge in Nepal is formed by Karnali River. Karnali is the longest river in Nepal (507 km). It is due to the high velocity of the river that it creates many gorges. Canyon- Canyons are the more eroded version of gorges. Grand Canyon is located in Arizona (US). It is a steep-sided canyon carved by Colorado River. The canyon is 446/447 km long with an average width of 6.4 to 29 km and depth of 1.8 km deep.

V-shaped Valley- V-shaped valleys are formed by erosion. The majority of the rivers in the world carry on two processes simultaneously i.e. vertical and horizontal erosion respectively. These rivers create V-shaped valleys.

Waterfalls- A waterfall is a stream that falls from a height. Waterfalls are often the sites of the greatest concentration of energy dissipation along the course of a stream.

Meanders- As water flowing under gravity seldom flows straight for any long distance, a winding course soon appears. The irregularities of the ground force the river to swing in loops, forming meanders.

Alluvial Cones - Also called alluvial fans, they are cone shaped deposits of sediments built by a stream where it merges into a broad valley or plain.

Delta- When the river reaches the sea, the fine materials it has not yet dropped are deposited at its mouth, forming a fan-shaped alluvial area called a delta. This alluvial tract is, in fact, a seaward extension of the floodplains. Deltas differ much in size, shape, growth and importance. A number of factors such as the rate of sedimentation the depth of the river, the sea bed and the character of tides, currents and waves greatly influence the eventual formation of deltas. The Ganges Delta is the largest delta in the world. It is also known as Ganges-Brahmaputra, Meghna Delta or Sunderban Delta.

Delta formation depends on sea depth: deltas need heavy sediment, slow flow, a gentle sea floor and a shallow sea or shelf; a deep sea hinders them.

The Islands

32 facts · 4 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (27 points)
  • An island is a piece of land surrounded on all sides by water. It may occur individually or in a group, in open oceans or seas. Smaller ones of only local significance are found even in lakes and rivers. Islands can be grouped under the following types- (a) Continental Islands (b) Oceanic Islands.
  • Greenland is the world’s largest (2166086 sq. km.) island. Greenland is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.
  • Nuuk is the capital and the largest city of Greenland. Nuuk has an elevation of1-3 m above sea level.
  • New Guinea is the second largest (785753 sq. km.) island in the world, located north of Australia. It is separated from the Australian mainland by Torres Strait.
  • Borneo is the third largest island in the world and the largest in Asia, located north of Java Sea. The island is politically divided among three countries- Indonesia (73%), Malaysia (26%) and Brunei (1%). The Kalimantan region of Indonesia is a part of Borneo islands.
  • Madagascar is an island country located in the Southwestern Indian Ocean, off the coast of East Africa. To the east of Madagascar, we have the island country of Mauritius and to the west, we have the African country of Mozambique. Madagascar is the fourth largest (587041 sq. km.) island in the world.
  • Diego Garcia is an island in the Indian Ocean. The island is named after the Portuguese explorer Diego Garcia who discovered it in the early 16th century. From 1814 to 1965 the island was a part of colonial Mauritius, later it became a dependency of the British Colony. In 1966, the United Kingdom leased it to the United States. At present, Diego Garcia is an active military base far the both US and UK.
  • Seychelles is an island situated to the north of Madagascar in the Indian Ocean. The island group comprises 115 islands, some of which are made up of corals and granite.
  • The Chagos Islands are located in the Indian Ocean. Diego Garcia is the largest island of Chagos Archipelago.
  • Mauritius is an island nation, located to the east of Madagascar in the Indian Ocean.
  • Socotra Island is located in the Indian Ocean between 12°30’ North latitude and 54° East Longitude. The island is officially a part of Yemen.
  • The island of Indonesia extends from Aceh in the west to Torres Strait (a Strait that lies between Australia and the Melanesian island of New Guinea) in the east. Indonesia is an island country in Southeast Asia between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. There are 17508 islands in Indonesia. Out of the 17508 islands only 1000 have been inhabited.
  • Fiji is an island country in the Pacific Ocean. Fiji lies to the east of Vanuatu, west of Tonga and the south of Tuvalu.
  • Fiji comprises 333 islands but approx. 87% of its population is concentrated on two islands Viti Levu and Vanua Levu.
  • The Falkland Archipelago is an Island group in South Atlantic Ocean, located at a distance of 650 km from the mainland of South America.
  • The Azores Island are an autonomous region of Portugal.
  • Cape Verde Island and the Bahamas are located in the Atlantic Ocean.
  • Macau is located approx. 64 km to the west of Hong Kong and is attached to mainland China.
  • Grenada is an island country in the southeastern caribbean Sea. Grenada consists of three islands - Grenada, carriacou and Petite Martinique which form the southern end of the Windward Islands. The island is also known as ‘Island of Spices’ because of the heavy production of the same. The island is located on the North Coast of Venezuela at a distance of 160 km.
  • The Balearic Islands are an archipelago of Spain in the western Mediterranean Sea. It is an autonomous community and a province of Spain. The flag of the Balearic Islands is distinct from that of Spain. The Balearic archipelago consists of 4 major islands. The capital of this island is Palma de Mallorca. Balearic island was a part of Spain since 1833 A.D. but in 1983 they became an autonomous region.
  • Melanesia is a sub-region of Oceania extending from Papua New Guinea in the South western Pacific Ocean to the Arafura Sea and then eastward to Fiji. The important islands of the region are- New Guinea, Bismarck Archipelago, Santa Cruz Islands, Vanuatu, Solomon, Fiji and New Caledonia.
  • The Australian continent is an island continent. It is the smallest continent and is completely under thejurisdiction of the sovereign state of Australia.
  • Japan is located in the Pacific Ocean to the east of the Asian mainland. It is a country of about 14125 islands (at least 100m circumference) of these only four are large and important. In the middle is Honshu occupying an area of 228000 km² and in the southwestern part the islands of Kyushu and Shikoku are located.

Key facts from the book (59 points)
  • Lakes are among the most varied features of the earth’s surface. They occupy the hollow of the land surface in which water accumulates.
  • Important lakes of the world include
  • – Caspian Sea, Lake Chad, lakes of U.S.A. and Canada (Lake Superior, Michigan Huron, Erie and Ontario), Lake Victoria, Aral Sea, Lake Nyasa, Lake Baikal, Great Bear Lake, Lake Titicaca, Dead Sea, Lake Crater, etc. Based on the total area occupied and volume, the largest lake in the world is the Caspian Sea of Eurasia. The lake covers an area of 371000 km². Caspian is a brackish water lake. The Ural and Volga rivers drain into its northern part. To the south of the Caspian Sea is the Kara-Bogaz Bay which has a salinity of approx 300-350‰. The Great Lakes of North America are located in the east-central part of the continent.
  • Lake Superior is the world’s largest freshwater Lake (Note - Lake Huron and Michigan are technically a single lake. On this basis lake Huron-Michigan is the largest freshwater lake by surface area in the world). It is one of the great lakes located between USA and Canada.
  • Lake Baikal of Russia is the World’s deepest lake having a maximum depth of 1642 meter. Baikal is about 25 million years old. Lake Baikal is also known as the Sacred Sea.
  • Lake Tanganyika is the world’s second deepest lake at 1470 meters. It is also the world’s longest freshwater lake (670 km).
  • Lake Titicaca is located on the border of Peru and Bolivia. It is the highest navigable lake in the world. It is 280 meters (919 feet) deep.
  • Lake Victoria is located between Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya.
  • The Dead Sea is a salt lake bordered by Jordan, Israel and Palestine (West Bank occupied by Israel).
  • The Aral Sea is a salt water lake on the borders of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Lake Van is the most saline lake in the world, with salinity reaching as high as 330‰ (according to Savindra Singh Book). Lake Van is located in Turkiye. Great Slave, Great Bear, Reindeer, Winnipeg, and Athabasca are some of the important lakes in Canada.
  • Uranium City is located near Lake Athabasca.
  • Boiling Lake is located in Dominica.
  • Red Lagoon is in Bolivia close to the Chilean border and Lake Urmia is in Iran.
  • Finger Lakes are a group of small lakes located in New York State.
  • Five Flower Lake is located in Sichuan Province China.
  • Finland is a Nordic country located in Northern Europe. Finland is known as the 'Garden of Lakes'/'Land of Thousand Lakes'.
  • Lake Saimaa is the largest lake in Finland and fourth largest natural freshwater lake in Europe. Cities that are located near the Great Lakes of North America are – Duluth near Lake Superior (North America), Chicago near Lake Michigan, and Buffalo near Lake Erie. The city of Detroit is located on the banks of Detroit River.

Lakes are water bodies surrounded by land on all sides. They vary tremendously in size, shape, depth and mode of formation. Hence keeping in mind the various competitive examinations, the following relevant facts have been provided regarding lakes-

WORLD

By volume-Lake Baikal,

by the total surface area covered - Lake Superior.

LAGOON

A lagoon is a body of water separated from larger bodies of water by a natural barrier. Natural barriers may include sandbars, barrier reefs, coral reefs, etc. Chilika (Odisha) is the largest lagoon in India whereas the New Caledonian barrier reef (in New Caledonia an overseas region of France) is the largest lagoon in the world.

The Atmosphere

15 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (11 points)
  • ∗The atmosphere is made up of different gases. Among all these gases oxygen and carbon dioxide are important for the existence of humans and plants respectively.
  • The atmosphere is composed of various gases, of which 99% is made up of nitrogen and oxygen. Other 1% comprises argon, carbon dioxide, neon, krypton, helium, Hydrogen, and xenon.

Gas Formula Presence in Atmosphere (in percentage)

NitrogenN₂78.084
OxygenO₂20.947
ArgonAr0.934
Carbon dioxideCO₂0.0426
NeonNe0.0018
HeliumHe0.0005
KryptonKr0.0001
HydrogenH₂0.000053
